When blanching, watch the water level carefully; do not let it boil over to avoid danger.
After blanching, it is recommended to rinse the chicken livers in cold water, or preferably ice water, to improve the texture.

mon_an.mo_ta: This Hunan-style small-fry dish uses high heat to quickly sear the beef, locking in its tenderness while releasing the aroma of the chilies. It features a bold, fresh spiciness and crunchy celery, embodying the essence of Hunan cuisine. Beef tenderloin provides high-quality protein and easily absorbed iron, while celery adds fiber for a balanced meal. The preparation and cooking steps are simple and clear—entirely stir-fried over high heat—making it very beginner-friendly. From prep to serving, it takes about an hour.
cac_buoc: Slice the beef tenderloin into thin pieces no more than 3cm wide and 3mm thick. Mix well with 6ml of soy sauce and set aside.
Cut the celery into sections no longer than 5cm and set aside.
Julienne the bird's eye chilies and set aside.
Finely dice the pickled wild chilies and set aside.
Cut the cilantro into sections no longer than 3cm and set aside.
Heat the wok, add 15ml of cooking oil, and wait for 30 seconds over high heat until the oil is hot.
Add the bird's eye chilies and pickled wild chilies, sautéing until fragrant.
Add the beef and celery, then **stir-fry over high heat for 1 minute**.
Turn off the heat, garnish with cilantro, and serve.
Maintain high heat throughout the entire cooking process.

mon_an.ten: Stir-Fried Pork with Bird's Eye Chilies
mon_an.mo_ta: This spicy and aromatic stir-fried pork is a classic Southwest Chinese dish that pairs perfectly with rice. The tender fresh pork combined with the refreshing heat of bird's eye chilies is incredibly appetizing. Pork is rich in protein and fat, while chilies provide plenty of vitamin C to stimulate the appetite. Although heat control is important when sautéing aromatics and stir-frying, the steps are clear and easy for beginners. Expect it to take about 25 minutes. Note: This dish is very spicy and is not recommended for those who prefer mild flavors.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Bird's eye chilies 20 pieces (adjust to taste)
cac_buoc: Wash the bird's eye chilies and slice them into slightly large diagonal pieces.
For the pork, either julienne or slice it as preferred. Marinate for 5 minutes with light soy sauce, oyster sauce, and salt.
Heat the wok with oil, stir-fry the pork until cooked through, then remove and set aside.

Sauté the ginger and garlic until fragrant, add the doubanjiang and stir-fry, then add the sliced chilies and the pork. Stir-fry briefly and season with a bit of light soy sauce, chicken bouillon, salt, and sugar.
**Seasonings can be adjusted to your preference; you can also add dark soy sauce for a richer aroma!**

mon_an.ten: Crispy Fried Pork Strips (Xiao Su Rou)
mon_an.mo_ta: Crispy on the outside and tender on the inside, these savory pork strips carry the signature numbing hint of Sichuan peppercorns. This is a classic home-style fried dish known to every household in the Sichuan-Chongqing region. Pork is rich in protein and fat, and since it is deep-fried, it is relatively high in calories—perfect for an occasional treat. This recipe involves several steps, requiring good heat control for the initial fry to set the shape and the second fry for color. It is slightly challenging for beginners and takes about 1 hour and 30 minutes from start to finish.
cac_buoc: Prepare the scallion and ginger water.
Julienne the ginger; leave the scallions whole.
Add the cooking wine and water according to the measurements.
Squeeze and knead the aromatics by hand for 5 minutes to fully release the scallion and ginger flavors into the water.
Prepare the pork.
Remove the pork skin and wash the meat.
Cut into strips 8-10 cm long and 1.5 cm thick.
Add salt, thirteen-spice powder, pepper powder, MSG, chicken bouillon, crushed Sichuan peppercorns, whole Sichuan peppercorns, and light soy sauce according to the recipe.
Pour in the prepared scallion and ginger water.
Massage and knead thoroughly for 10 minutes until the meat absorbs all the liquid and becomes sticky.
Cover with plastic wrap and let it rest in the refrigerator for 30 minutes.
Coat the pork.
Add the flour and sweet potato starch to the marinated meat, then add the egg whites.
Knead thoroughly for 15 minutes.
First fry to set the shape.
Pour vegetable oil into a wok. Control the amount based on the wok size, ensuring the oil depth is over 3 cm.
Heat over high heat to 150°C, then turn to low heat to maintain the temperature.

Use chopsticks to drop the coated pork strips into the oil, smoothing them into your desired shape. Fry for 3-5 minutes to set. They are ready when they look slightly golden and feel firm when touched with a spatula. The exact time depends on the size of the strips, oil temperature, and thickness of the batter.
Remove and drain. Tip: If unsure about the time, fry a bit longer to avoid a raw smell. Beginners can add strips one by one to prevent sticking.
Second fry for the final result.
Increase the oil temperature to 180°C. Return the fried strips to the wok and fry until golden brown, then remove.
When coating, make sure to break up any lumps in the sweet potato starch; do not leave dry pockets of starch inside, or they will explode in the oil!!!
If you have leftovers, you can stop after the first fry and refrigerate them. Simply re-fry them later; the taste will remain largely the same.

mon_an.mo_ta: This dish is fresh, spicy, and appetizing, featuring tender and succulent bullfrog meat—a typical Sichuan home-style dish. Bullfrog is high in protein and low in fat. Combined with pickled ginger, pickled chilies, and other fermented ingredients, it is incredibly flavorful. The method is relatively straightforward, but requires attention to oil temperature and seasoning ratios. Beginners can usually complete this in 1 to 2 hours.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Bullfrog meat, cut into pieces 800g (buy 1.5kg of live bullfrog; small ones are recommended for tender meat)
Pickled ginger 20-30 gram (adjust to taste; use more for a bolder flavor)
Pickled chilies 5-10 gram (adjust based on heat tolerance; 2.5g is recommended for a mild-medium heat)
Garlic 30-50 gram (adjust to taste, but at least 30g is recommended)
Doubanjiang (spicy bean paste) 20-30 gram (30g for bold flavor, 20g for milder. PS: This dish shouldn't be too mild, haha)
Tapioca starch 30 gram (dry cornstarch can be substituted)
Lard 20ml (optional; can substitute with cooking oil)
cac_buoc: Clean the bullfrog meat and drain. Add at least 10g of salt and 50ml of beer, then massage by hand for 5 minutes to remove any fishy odor.
Rinse with clean water until the water runs clear of blood and impurities. Drain well and place in a bowl for marinating.
Add 5g of salt, 30g of tapioca starch, 10ml of cooking wine, and 5g of pepper powder. Mix well by hand and marinate for 5-10 minutes.
Cut the pickled ginger, pickled chilies, and pickled wild chilies into strips or slices. Slice the green and red chilies into rings. Peel the garlic cloves.

Heat a wok and add 200ml of cooking oil (add an extra 100ml if using a flat-bottomed pan). Heat until about 160°C (small bubbles appear), add the marinated bullfrog, and flash-fry quickly. Remove after 10 seconds (do not overcook or the meat will become dry and tough).
After removing the bullfrog and draining the oil, pour the hot oil into a bowl, leaving 30ml in the wok. Add 20ml of lard (or just keep 50ml of cooking oil in total).

When the oil is hot, add the pickled ginger, pickled chilies, pickled wild chilies, and garlic. Sauté until fragrant, then add 20g of doubanjiang. Stir-fry over medium heat for 30 seconds until the oil turns red. Pour in 400ml of beer.
Add the flash-fried bullfrog. Use a spatula to gently push and turn the meat—do not stir vigorously. Add 5g of pepper powder and 5ml of rattan pepper oil. Simmer over medium heat for 3 minutes.
Increase to high heat and reduce the sauce for half a minute. Add the green and red chili rings and cook for another 10 seconds before serving.
Transfer to a serving bowl, garnish with chopped scallions, and enjoy!
When draining the meat, you can use a slotted spoon to press out excess liquid.
When applying the starch, ensure every piece of bullfrog is evenly coated.

mon_an.ten: Stir-Fried Beef with Long Green Peppers
mon_an.mo_ta: A savory and slightly spicy home-style stir-fry featuring tender, flavorful beef and crisp, refreshing long green peppers. Beef provides high-quality protein and iron, while the peppers are rich in vitamin C, making for a nutritionally balanced meal. While the marinating process requires some patience, the steps are clear and manageable for beginners. Total time from prep to serving is about 1 hour.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Calculate the ingredient ratios based on the conditions above.
cac_buoc: Prepare the aromatics and sides.
Mince the garlic.
Cut the scallions into sections.
Slice the ginger.
Cut the long green peppers into sections.
Pre-process the beef.
Place the beef in a bowl.
Add the ginger, salt, soy sauce, and sugar. Marinate for 30-40 minutes.
Remove the ginger slices after marinating.
Stir-fry.
Add oil to a cold wok and heat until bubbles occasionally appear.
Add the minced garlic.
Once the garlic is golden, add the long green peppers.
When the pepper skins are slightly blistered, add the marinated beef and stir-fry.
Just before the beef is fully cooked, add the scallions and continue stir-frying.
Once the beef is cooked through, turn off the heat and serve.
You can add baking soda during marination to tenderize the beef (ratio: 3g baking soda per 500g beef).
The ginger slices in the marinade can be replaced with cooking wine (3g per person).

mon_an.mo_ta: Guo You Rou is a famous traditional dish from Shanxi, featuring tender pork slices and crisp garlic sprouts with a savory, fresh, and slightly sour flavor profile highlighted by the rich aroma of aged black vinegar. It is a quintessential local home-style dish. Pork tenderloin provides high-quality protein, combined with wood ear mushrooms, garlic sprouts, and shallots for balanced nutrition. This dish requires specific heat control and starch-coating techniques, making it a great challenge for those with some cooking experience. Total time from preparation to serving is about 40 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: I have a big appetite; this is my portion for one person
cac_buoc: Soak the wood ear mushrooms until expanded; if in a hurry, use hot water.

Slice the pork tenderloin and place in a bowl. Add 20ml of light soy sauce, cooking wine, Sichuan peppercorn powder, and one egg. Mix well by hand, then add starch (sweet potato starch recommended) and mix again. Pour in 300ml of cooking oil to coat and marinate for 15 minutes.
Cut the garlic sprouts into 3cm segments and the shallots into diamond-shaped pieces; set aside.
Heat a generous amount of oil in a wok. When the oil is about 50% hot (medium heat), add the marinated pork slices. Separate the slices, then remove and drain; set aside.
Pour out the excess oil, leaving only 10ml for stir-frying. Heat until about 70% hot (medium-high heat).

Sauté the scallion, ginger, and garlic until fragrant. Add the garlic sprouts and stir-fry until just tender, then add the wood ear mushrooms and shallots. Pour in the light soy sauce and Sichuan peppercorn powder. Toss a few times, then add the fried pork slices and stir-fry together.
Add 10g of salt. Just before serving, add 10ml of vinegar and chicken bouillon powder, then transfer to a plate.
When frying the pork slices, aim for a slightly seared surface; pay close attention to the heat control.
You can also add a thin starch slurry before serving for a better texture.

mon_an.mo_ta: This Pakistani-style beef curry is richly aromatic, tender, and savory with a tangy and spicy kick. The beef provides high-quality protein, while tomatoes and yogurt ensure balanced nutrition. The method is straightforward, though the slow simmering requires some patience—perfect for a relaxed weekend preparation. In about two and a half hours, you will have a warm, exotic pot of deliciousness.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: The measurements here are based on 1kg of beef; adjust accordingly. Curry made from 1kg of beef serves approximately 5 people.
cac_buoc: Cut all the spiral chilies into segments; set aside.
Blend all the tomatoes into a puree; set aside.
Cut the beef into 2cm cubes, wash thoroughly, and set aside.
Add a layer of oil to a wok (to prevent the tomato puree from splattering while boiling).
Add the tomato puree and stir constantly for 2-3 minutes until it turns a deeper red.
Add 5g of garlic powder, 5g of ginger powder, and 1 pack (50g) of Masala powder; stir well.
Add the beef and chili segments; stir well.
Add 1 container of yogurt (to thicken the sauce); stir well.
Transfer the entire mixture to an electric rice cooker or slow cooker. Add 250 ml of water and set to the meat stew or slow cook mode for 2-3 hours.
Once finished, check if the beef is tender and serve.
This recipe was learned from a Pakistani friend and has been specifically refined; it is absolutely authentic.
Usually served with roti, naan, or rice.
To make Chicken Karahi, the process is nearly identical, except you should first fry the chicken with oil and peppercorns until golden brown.

mon_an.ten: Dali Braised Pork Shank (Dai Ba Zhou Zi)
mon_an.mo_ta: Dali Braised Pork Shank is a famous traditional dish from Dali, Shaanxi, named for its handle-like shape. The finished dish features tender, chewy skin and melt-in-your-mouth meat that isn't greasy. It is served with sweet bean sauce and scallion sections for a rich, savory flavor. High in collagen and quality protein, it is both nutritious and skin-beautifying. This recipe requires deboning, shaping, and long steaming, which may be challenging for beginners. The entire process takes about 3.5 hours.
cac_buoc: Clean and scrape the pork shank. Place it on a cutting board with the top of the shank facing away from you, the trotter facing toward you, and the skin side down.

Use a knife to slit the skin down the center from the top toward the trotter along the leg bone. Separate the meat from both sides of the bone (detaching meat on three sides) while keeping the bottom bone attached to the meat to expose the bone. Then, use the back of a knife (or a cleaver) to break the two middle leg joints.

Place the shank in a pot and boil until 70% cooked (the outside looks normal but the inside is still light pink). Remove and pat dry with a clean towel. While still hot, rub the dark soy sauce onto the skin.

Prepare a steamer. Place star anise and cinnamon at the bottom. Break the shank joint by hand without damaging the outer skin, then place the shank into the steamer skin-side down. Depending on the size of the shank, curl the trotter end tightly against the wall of the pot to form a circular shape.

Sprinkle with fine salt and cover the meat with a layer of sterilized clean gauze. Spread the sweet bean sauce (50g), scallions (75g), red fermented bean curd, dark soy sauce, light soy sauce, ginger, and garlic over the gauze. Steam over high heat for about 3 hours (until the meat is fork-tender).

Once steamed, remove from the heat, discard the gauze, and flip the shank onto a plate. Remove the star anise. Serve with a small side dish of scallion sections and sweet bean sauce (alternatively, spread the sweet bean sauce over the shank and serve with scallions on the side).
Judging when the shank is 70% cooked requires practical experience; if possible, consult an experienced cook.
Fill the bottom of the steamer with water and place the shank in the top section. Be sure to add water periodically during steaming to prevent the pot from boiling dry.

mon_an.mo_ta: This is a creative Sichuan-style dish with a sweet and spicy flavor originating from the Peking University canteen. The chicken is marinated and then fried until crispy on the outside and tender on the inside, paired with floury potatoes and crisp green peppers, all coated in a glossy, sweet, and spicy sauce. It is rich in protein, starch, and vitamins. This dish involves deep-frying and sauce reduction, which can be a bit challenging for beginners, but following the steps will ensure success. The process takes about 1 hour.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Pixian red oil broad bean paste: 40g
cac_buoc: Debone the chicken thighs (skip if using pre-deboned meat). Use the back of a knife to pound the meat a few times, then cut into 2cm pieces.

Add salt, chicken powder (optional), pepper powder, light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, and cooking wine to the chicken. Mix until the meat becomes sticky, then add starch and mix well. Add a little cooking oil to prevent sticking and marinate for 30 minutes.
Peel the potatoes and cut into 2cm pieces. Boil in water for 5 minutes, then remove and drain thoroughly to prevent oil splattering during frying.
Deseed the green peppers, cut into 2cm pieces, and set aside in a mesh strainer.
Add plenty of oil to a wok (enough to submerge the ingredients). When the oil reaches 180°C, add the potatoes and fry for 3 minutes, then remove.
When the oil returns to 180°C, add the chicken and fry for 2 minutes, then remove.
When the oil returns to 180°C again, fry the chicken a second time for 1 minute, then remove.
When the oil returns to 180°C once more, fry the potatoes a second time for 1 minute. Then, pour the oil and potatoes through the mesh strainer containing the green peppers to flash-cook the peppers.

Heat 5ml of oil in the wok over low heat. Sauté the garlic cloves until golden, then add the broad bean paste and stir-fry until fragrant. Add the white sugar and stir until melted, then add the crushed Sichuan peppercorns and 40ml of water. Stir constantly until the sauce thickens.
Add the fried chicken, potatoes, and green peppers. Toss well to coat and serve.
If you prefer not to deep-fry, you can use less oil to pan-fry the chicken and potatoes. This will take longer and slightly affect the texture, but the overall flavor will remain delicious.

mon_an.ten: Cantonese Braised Beef Brisket with Radish
mon_an.mo_ta: This is a classic Cantonese home-style stew: the beef brisket is braised until tender and flavorful, while the radish absorbs the sweet and savory sauce. It is rich in quality protein and fiber, making it an appetizing dish that aids digestion. Although there are several steps, the difficulty is moderate, and beginners can succeed by following the sequence. The process takes about 2.5 hours from start to finish.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Scallions: 1 bunch, tied in a knot
Red fermented bean curd (Nam Yu): 1 piece
cac_buoc: Begin preparation.
Cut the radish into rolling chunks and set aside.
Blanch the whole piece of beef brisket with 2 slices of ginger and the scallion knot. Once the water boils, cook for 5-10 minutes, then remove and slice.
Cut the brisket into pieces of your preferred size (since it has been blanched, it won't shrink much during braising; larger pieces will just need a bit more time).

Prepare the braising sauce by mixing the red fermented bean curd, Chu Hou paste, soy sauce, oyster sauce, sugar, and salt according to the quantities above (white sugar can be used if rock sugar is unavailable).

Heat oil in a pan and sauté the ginger and garlic until fragrant. Add the beef brisket and stir-fry until the surface is dry. Pour in the prepared sauce and stir-fry until aromatic. Add a little dark soy sauce if a deeper color is desired.
Once the seasonings are evenly combined, pour in hot water.
Transfer the brisket to a soup pot. Add the cinnamon, star anise, bay leaves, and dried chilies. Braise for about 2 hours.
When the brisket is halfway tender, add the white radish and continue to braise for 30 minutes.
Once the radish is soft and tender, the dish is ready. You now have a pot of rich, aromatic beef brisket with radish.

mon_an.ten: Huizhou-style Braised Pork (Huizhou Hong Shao Rou)
mon_an.mo_ta: Huizhou-style Braised Pork is a classic Huizhou family dish with a glossy red color. It is rich but not greasy, tender yet chewy, with a perfect balance of sweet and savory. The main ingredient is pork belly, which is rich in high-quality protein and fat, providing plenty of energy. The cooking process requires mastering the sugar caramelization and heat control, which can be a bit challenging. Estimated cooking time is about 45 minutes.
cac_buoc: Cut the pork belly into 2-3 cm cubes.
Heat 150 ml of oil in a pan, add the pork belly and fry for 2 minutes. Add salt, stir-fry the pork, and remove from the pan after 2 minutes.
Heat 50 ml of oil in the pan, add the white sugar, and stir-fry until it turns a coffee-brown color.
Add the pork belly and stir-fry for 30 seconds. Add the ginger slices and garlic, then stir-fry for another 30 seconds.
Add the cooking wine, five-spice powder, and scallion. Add enough water to cover the pork, cover with a lid, and cook for 10 minutes.
Add the light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, and oyster sauce. Cook over medium heat for 20 minutes.
Remove the lid, increase to high heat to reduce the sauce, and serve on a plate.
Keep the scallion stalk whole; there is no need to chop it.
The purpose of adding salt in step two is to help the pork belly retain its fat.
During the process, you can boil one portion of the pork belly first and then follow the steps with the unboiled portion; you will find the unboiled meat is crispier and chewier.

mon_an.mo_ta: Italian-style Roasted Chicken is a Mediterranean-flavored home oven dish. Chicken thighs are marinated in garlic-infused olive oil; once roasted, the skin is slightly charred while the inside remains tender and juicy. Combined with lemon juice and parsley, the taste is refreshing and not greasy. Chicken is rich in high-quality protein, and olive oil provides unsaturated fatty acids for balanced nutrition. The difficulty is moderate; the oven needs to be preheated. Beginners can complete it smoothly by following the steps. Total time from marinating to serving is about fifty minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Use the above conditions to calculate the ratio of ingredients intended for use.
cac_buoc: Pre-process the chicken.
Rub salt, black pepper, olive oil, and minced garlic onto the chicken thighs.
Place in a preheated oven at 180°C and roast for 30-40 minutes or until cooked through.
Prepare the seasonings.
Finely chop the parsley and set aside.
Squeeze the lemon juice and set aside.
Roasting.
Remove the roasted chicken and drizzle with lemon juice.
Sprinkle with chopped parsley to finish.
While roasting, you can drizzle honey or other BBQ sauces on the chicken to enhance the flavor.
Preheat the oven to 180°C; roasting time depends on the size and thickness of the chicken, ensuring it is fully cooked.
Chicken must be completely cooked before eating; consuming undercooked chicken can cause food poisoning and infections from bacteria such as Salmonella and Shigella.

mon_an.ten: Xinjiang Big Plate Chicken (Xinjiang Da Pan Ji)
mon_an.mo_ta: Xinjiang Big Plate Chicken is a hearty Xinjiang family dish with vibrant colors: the chicken is tender and not dry, and the potatoes are soft, absorbing the sauce with a numbing-spicy flavor and a hint of sweetness. It is rich in high-quality protein and starch, and the addition of bell peppers provides vitamin C. The process requires caramelizing sugar and mastering the heat to reduce the sauce, which is a bit challenging for beginners, but not difficult if you follow the steps carefully. It takes about 1 hour in total.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Bell pepper and sweet pepper: 1 each, 50 g each
cac_buoc: Chop the meat into cubes, soak in clean water with salt for 5 minutes to remove blood and gamey odors, then drain.
Wash the scallions, garlic, peppers, and potatoes; peel the potatoes.
Cut the white parts of the scallions into 4 cm lengths; cut the bell peppers and sweet peppers into chunks.
Cut the potatoes into wedges using a rolling cut (cut once, rotate the potato, and cut again), about 4 cm * 4 cm per piece.
Caramelize the sugar: first add oil to the pan, then add white sugar. Stir with a spatula until the sugar melts and turns a burnt yellow color, then add the drained chicken to the pan to color it.
Add Sichuan peppercorns, bay leaves, black cardamom, and dried long chilies, and stir-fry.
Add 5 g salt, 7 ml light soy sauce, 10 g oyster sauce, 100 g cooking wine, and pour in 1 liter of water. Cooking wine can be replaced with beer.
Adjust to medium heat, bring to a boil, then switch to medium-low heat and simmer slowly to let the flavors penetrate.

When the water has reduced and the chicken is almost visible, place the potatoes on top: note do not stir the potatoes, just layer them on top, otherwise they may stick to the bottom. Cover and continue to simmer. After a while, add the large scallions, bell peppers, and sweet peppers, and continue simmering.

When the water is almost gone, you can flip the ingredients to let the potatoes absorb the sauce, then turn off the heat and serve. **Additionally: this dish can be eaten with noodles. Buy large pieces of dough, flatten them, and pull by hand into wide noodles. They must be wide noodles; once boiled, add them to the big plate of chicken and mix with the sauce for an excellent taste!**

mon_an.ten: Boneless Chicken Feet (Wu Gu Ji Zhua)
mon_an.mo_ta: A spicy and sour appetizer, chewy and crunchy, this is a classic homemade cold-mixed snack. Chicken feet are rich in collagen, which is good for the skin. The deboning step is tedious and labor-intensive with a high difficulty level, making it less suitable for beginners. The entire process takes about 8 hours and 15 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Bird's eye chilies: 4 mild, 6 medium, 12 very spicy (very spicy recommended)
Black vinegar (aged black vinegar recommended) 50 g
Lemon 2 fruits (use 1 fruit as a unit to adjust acidity)
cac_buoc: Process the chicken feet.
Use scissors or a knife to cut off all the claws from the chicken feet, **including the meat and bone under the claws, so no trace of the claw remains.**
Rinse with water and set aside.
Place the `chicken feet` in a large pot to prepare for deodorizing.
Add all the `large scallions`, `cooking wine`, and `ginger`.
Add enough water to cover the `chicken feet`.
Bring to a boil over high heat; **you can skim off the foam in the middle.**
Once the water reaches **100 degrees boiling**, wait for 10 minutes.
Turn off the heat, remove, drain, rinse, and place in a basin. Deboning: this step can be skipped; it takes about 2 hours.
Place in the **freezer** for 20 minutes.
Move everything to the non-freezer section of the fridge, then take them out in batches of **10 at a time** to debone.
Starting from the tip of the toe, use a knife to make a slit **all the way to the metatarsus (top of the foot).**
Then, from the metatarsus, continue the slit all the way up the leg.
Snap each toe joint slightly **until you hear a popping sound.**
Press the tip of the toe and push inward; repeat for each toe, first pushing to the middle of the sole and top of the foot.
Once the skin of each toe is separated, push from the sole toward the leg until the entire bone is removed.
Place in a bowl and set aside. Prepare the marinade.
Finely chop the `bird's eye chilies` into even pieces.
Mince the `garlic`, `onion`, and `cilantro`.
Halve the `lemons` and squeeze the juice into the container with the chicken feet.
Pour `all` the seasonings into the container, adding the `chilies`, `garlic`, `onion`, and `cilantro`.
Toss and mix thoroughly.
Refrigerate overnight (6 hours).
Once the marinade is ready, pour it all over the prepared chicken feet.
When cooking, pay attention to the water level; if it falls below 3/4 of the ingredients, add hot water to submerge them.

mon_an.mo_ta: This is a classic stew originating from Northeast China, refreshing, sour, fresh, and fragrant—perfect for warming the heart and stomach. Sauerkraut is rich in lactic acid bacteria and fiber, ribs provide high-quality protein and calcium, and blood sausage supplements iron. Patience is needed when handling the blood sausage to prevent it from bursting during cooking, which is a bit challenging for beginners. From preparation to serving, it is expected to take about one hour.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: This dish is suitable for 2-3 people. Ingredients per portion:
Dipping sauce: chili oil 5 g, light soy sauce 10 g, minced garlic 5 g, sesame oil 2 g.
cac_buoc: Use a toothpick to prick many small holes in the blood sausage, then place it in water. Simmer over low heat for ten minutes; do not let the water boil, keep it at 80°C, otherwise the blood sausage will easily burst.
Slice the cooked blood sausage and set aside.
Blanch the ribs with cooking wine, drain, and set aside.
Heat rapeseed oil in a pan, add garlic cloves, dried chilies, and ginger powder, and sauté until fragrant.
Add the ribs and stir-fry until the surface is golden.
Rinse the sauerkraut and squeeze dry. Add it to the pan along with sesame oil. Sesame oil helps neutralize the acidity and makes the sauerkraut more fragrant. Stir-fry on high heat for two minutes.
Add 600 ml of hot water.
Transfer to an electric pressure cooker and add the bay leaves, star anise, scallion knot, and salt.
Set to the "extra fragrant" pressure mode for 40 minutes.

When the time is up, release the pressure and open the lid. Add the blood sausage and goji berries, cover and let it sit for two minutes. The blood sausage is already cooked and does not need further boiling.
Pour into a basin, prepare the dipping sauce according to the table above, and serve.

mon_an.ten: Lamb and Fried Tofu Skin Clay Pot (Zhi Zhu Yang Nan Bao)
mon_an.mo_ta: This is a traditional clay pot dish from Guangdong. Lamb and fried tofu skin (fuzhu) are simmered with Chu Hou paste and fermented bean curd, creating a rich savory flavor that is hearty but not greasy. It is warming and comforting, especially suitable for cold winter days. Lamb is rich in protein and iron, which can nourish the blood and warm the body, while tofu skin provides high-quality plant protein for balanced nutrition. Although there are many preparation and simmering steps, the heat control is not complex. Beginners can succeed by following the sequence. Total time from preparation to serving is about two and a half hours.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Red fermented bean curd (Nam Yu) 35 g
cac_buoc: Preparation: Soak shiitake mushrooms 2-3 hours in advance until soft. Soak tofu skin 30 minutes in advance until soft.
Prepare Sauce 1: In a small bowl, mix the red fermented bean curd, Chu Hou paste, 20 g of fermented bean curd, and dark soy sauce.
Prepare Sauce 2: In another small bowl, mix 20 g of fermented bean curd, white sugar, and chili oil.
Trim the stems off the soaked shiitake mushrooms.
Cut the soaked tofu skin into 5 cm segments and squeeze out excess water.
Peel and slice the onion. Shallots can also be used as a substitute for better flavor.
Cut the scallions into 5 cm lengths.
Place the lamb brisket in a pot of cold water with 2-3 ginger slices. Bring to a boil over high heat, then turn off the heat.
Remove the lamb and place it in a basin of cold water to cool, which helps make the meat chewier.
Heat the pan and add oil. Sauté 4-5 ginger slices, onion/shallots, scallion whites, and 7-8 garlic cloves until fragrant.
Add the cooled lamb brisket and stir with chopsticks for 2-5 minutes until it turns golden.
Add Sauce 1 and stir-fry for about 2 minutes until evenly coated.
Pour in clean water until the ingredients are just submerged.
Add the shiitake mushrooms, rock sugar, bay leaf, star anise, and cinnamon.
Cover and simmer over low heat for 90 minutes.
Open the lid, add the tofu skin, cover, and cook over medium heat for 20 minutes.
Open the lid, add Sauce 2, and stir well.
Turn off the heat. Before serving, add the green scallion tops or cilantro.
This is a Cantonese dish; authentic versions often include water chestnuts. Depending on personal preference for radishes or other greens, you can also substitute with potatoes or radishes.

mon_an.ten: Cantonese Chu Hou Beef Brisket (Chu Hou Ngau Nam)
mon_an.mo_ta: This is a classic Cantonese dish with a rich, fragrant aroma and a glossy red color. The beef brisket and tendons are simmered until tender and flavorful, offering a complex taste. It is rich in high-quality protein and collagen, making it nourishing and warming. While it requires patience, using a pressure cooker can significantly shorten the time, making it beginner-friendly. Traditional simmering takes about 3 hours, while a pressure cooker takes about 1 hour.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: The following is for a portion serving two people:
Bird's eye chili 1 piece (adjust to taste)
cac_buoc: First, prepare the secondary ingredients: Bowl 1: ginger cut into 1.5 cm cubes, half a bulb of peeled garlic, and chopped chili (if using). Bowl 2: 2 bay leaves, 0.5 g Sichuan peppercorns, 2 star anise, 3 dried chilies, 3 cloves, and 2 licorice slices. Bowl 3: 2 pieces of red fermented bean curd. Bowl 4: 15 g bean paste. Bowl 5: 10 g rock sugar. Bowl 6: 10 g Huadiao wine and 10 g white spirit. Bowl 7: 50 g Chu Hou paste, 20 g oyster sauce, 20 g char siu sauce, 5 g dark soy sauce, and 60 g light soy sauce.
Do not cut the beef yet. Place it directly into a pot of cold water and blanch over high heat. Once the water boils, remove the beef.
Wash away impurities from the surface of the beef, cut into large 4 cm * 4 cm * 4 cm cubes, drain, and set aside in a bowl.
Heat oil in a pan over high heat. Add Bowl 1 (ginger, garlic, chili) and sauté until fragrant.
Reduce to medium-low heat, add Bowl 2 (aromatics), and stir for about 30 seconds.
On medium-low heat, add Bowl 3 (red fermented bean curd) and use a spatula to mash it.
On medium-low heat, add Bowl 4 (bean paste) and stir for about 30 seconds.
On medium-low heat, add Bowl 5 (rock sugar) and stir until melted.
On medium-low heat, add the beef brisket and stir-fry until the beef is colored.
Increase to high heat, drizzle Bowl 6 (alcohol) along the edge of the pan, and stir-fry quickly until the beef surface is slightly browned.
Pour in Bowl 7 (sauce) and stir-fry quickly. Watch the liquid at the bottom; stir-fry until small bubbles continuously appear and the sauce thickens slightly.
Transfer all ingredients to a stew pot or pressure cooker and add water until submerged.
Choose the simmering time based on the pot used: a. Regular pot: simmer on low heat for 3 hours. b. Pressure cooker: pressure cook for 40 minutes.
When the time is up, open the lid and taste. If not salty enough, add salt or light soy sauce (add a little at a time and taste); if not sweet enough, add sugar.
After seasoning, you can remove the beef brisket first.

If you want to add radish or potatoes, peel and cut them into 2 cm thick slices. Add to the pot and cook for 10-15 minutes (or until desired tenderness). For a pressure cooker, cook for an additional 5 minutes under pressure.
Once cooked, combine the radish/potatoes with the beef.
Strain the sauce and pour it over the dish.
Please be careful when using a pressure cooker!

mon_an.ten: Guilin Eighteen Stuffed Dishes (Guilin Shiba Niang)
mon_an.mo_ta: A traditional series of stuffed dishes from Guilin: various seasoned fillings like pork or shrimp are stuffed into over ten types of hollow ingredients such as green peppers, bitter melon, river snails, and eggplant, then pan-fried and braised. Each dish has a unique flavor, juicy and fresh, with textures ranging from soft to chewy, representing a rich local family taste. The fillings provide high-quality protein, combined with various vegetables rich in vitamins and fiber for balanced nutrition. The steps involve stuffing each item individually and mastering the heat, requiring some patience, but the logic is simple enough for beginners to try. Total completion time is about 1.5 hours.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: 18 types of vessels × 4 types of fillings = 72 combinations; in practice, about 20 combinations are commonly used.
Core formula: **tubular vessel + meat filling + frying/braising = stuffed dish**
cac_buoc: Core Concept
The so-called "niang" (stuffing) involves finding a hollow, tubular ingredient to act as a vessel, stuffing it with seasoned meat filling, and then frying or braising it until cooked.
Taking two existing stuffed dishes as examples:
**Stuffed Green Peppers**: Deseed and hollow out green peppers → stuff with pork or shrimp filling → pan-fry until "tiger skin" (blistered) → braise with sauce.

**Stuffed River Snails**: Blanch snails to remove meat → mince snail meat and mix with pork → stuff back into the snail shells → braise with perilla and mint. Change to a different tubular ingredient and repeat the process to create a new dish. Stuffed bitter melon, stuffed eggplant, stuffed tofu... they all follow this logic. The filling (stuffing) can also be varied:
**Pork Filling**: The most common basic choice; a 3:7 fat-to-lean ratio provides the best flavor.
**Shrimp Filling**: Sweet, fresh, and bouncy; often used in stuffed green peppers.
**Snail and Pork Mix**: The soul of stuffed river snails; 1:1 ratio of snail meat to pork, with added perilla and mint.

**Mixed Filling**: A blend of pork and shrimp, both sweet-fresh and rich-savory. One vessel with one filling; change one, and you have a new stuffed dish. The local saying "everything can be stuffed" refers to this. Think of it this way: "vessels" (bitter melon, eggplant, tofu, shiitake, pumpkin blossoms, pomelo pith, bamboo shoots, winter melon, taro, garlic, tomato, bean sprouts, eggs...) and "fillings" (pork, shrimp, fish, mixed) are independent and can be freely combined. Change a vessel for a new dish; change a filling for a new variation.
Existing formulas:
Stuffed Green Peppers — pork-stuffed peppers / shrimp-stuffed peppers.
Stuffed River Snails — 1:1 snail and pork meat, with perilla and mint.

mon_an.ten: Braised Pork with Meigan Cai (Mei Cai Kou Rou)
mon_an.mo_ta: This is a famous traditional Hakka dish. The final product is a glossy soy-red color with a thick sauce. The pork is incredibly tender and fragrant, rich but not greasy. Pork belly provides high-quality protein and fatty acids, while the dried Meigan cai provides fiber. The overall process has several steps, requiring mastery of heat during boiling, frying, and steaming, which is a bit challenging for beginners. From preparation to serving, including the soaking time for the greens, it takes about 2.5 hours.
cac_buoc: Soak the Meigan cai in clean water for 1 hour.
Heat 50 ml of oil in a pan, place the whole piece of pork belly skin-side down for 1 minute, then remove and scrape the skin clean [optional].
Add boiling water to the pan, add the pork belly, and cook on high heat for 20 minutes (until a chopstick can pierce the meat), then remove the pork.
Rub dark soy sauce, five-spice powder, and white sugar evenly onto the surface of the pork belly and let it sit for 15 minutes.
Heat oil in a pan, add the pork belly, and fry over medium heat until both sides are golden (3-5 minutes).
Heat oil in a pan, add the Meigan cai, bird's eye chili, minced garlic, chicken bouillon, and salt. Stir-fry until the moisture in the dried greens has evaporated.
Slice the pork belly (leaving 0.5-1 cm at the end), arrange in a large bowl, and spread the Meigan cai on top.
Steam over medium heat for 45 minutes.
Place a plate upside down over the bowl of pork belly and invert the pork onto the plate.
During the process, the crispy pork skin smells amazing Orz~
If you don't like sweetness, you can omit the white sugar; it won't affect the main process.
The steaming time in the penultimate step can be adjusted to personal preference.
The purpose of stir-frying the Meigan cai dry is to help it absorb the oil later (just a guess).

mon_an.ten: Salt and Pepper Pork Ribs (Xiao Yan Pai Diao)
mon_an.mo_ta: Salt and Pepper Pork Ribs is a classic Shanghai home dish, crispy on the outside and tender on the inside, with a savory and fragrant taste. Pork chops provide high-quality protein and essential amino acids to boost physical strength. Although there are several steps, it is not difficult if you follow the process, so beginners can confidently give it a try. From preparation to serving takes about 40 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Before starting, determine how many servings to make. One portion is enough for 1-2 people.
Custard powder 2-3 g (for color and aroma; optional)
cac_buoc: Wash the pork chops, remove the bones, pound with the back of a knife to tenderize, cut into thick slices, and then into thick strips.
Add salt and pepper powder, mix well, and once it becomes tacky, add the ginger-scallion water **one bit at a time**. Marinate in the refrigerator for 20 minutes.
Make the batter. Combine 80 g flour, 20 g starch (note: 20 g starch here, keep the remaining 60 g aside), 2-3 g custard powder, and 1 g salt.
Crack in an egg, whisk, then add 100 g of water gradually, followed by 10 g of oil, whisking continuously until the batter is smooth and slightly thick.
Take the remaining 60 g of starch. Take a pork strip, coat it in a layer of starch, then dip it into the batter.

Add enough oil to a pan to submerge the ingredients and heat to about 150°C - 160°C. Fry the pork strips until light yellow, then remove. They might stick when first added; do not touch them. Once they set, use chopsticks to flip and separate them.
When the oil reaches 150°C - 160°C again, fry the strips a second time until golden brown, then remove.
Sprinkle with salt and pepper powder, toss well, and serve.
Breadcrumbs can be used instead of batter, but the taste is quite different.
The batter can also be used for frying chicken thighs, fish, etc.

mon_an.ten: Szechuan Poached Beef (Shui Zhu Niu Rou)
mon_an.mo_ta: Szechuan Poached Beef is a classic spicy and numbing dish from Szechuan cuisine: tender meat, a glossy red sauce, and a hot, fresh, aromatic flavor. The beef is rich in high-quality protein and iron, paired with bean sprouts for added fiber. This dish is not too difficult for beginners, but requires attention to the heat and safety when drizzling the hot oil; the total process takes about forty minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine the number of servings before starting. One serving is enough for 2 people.
cac_buoc: Wash the beef and slice thinly.
Add 15g julienned ginger, 1 egg, 15g starch, 8g oyster sauce, and 10ml cooking wine to a bowl; stir well and marinate for 15 minutes.
Wash and finely chop the cilantro.
Add oil to a pan, then add the Doubanjiang, 5g julienned ginger, and sliced garlic.
Pour in boiling water to create a red broth.
Wash the bean sprouts, remove the roots, and blanch in boiling water until cooked.
Spread the bean sprouts at the bottom of a large bowl.
Add the beef slices one by one into the red broth, cook until done, then remove.
Place the beef on top of the bean sprouts and sprinkle with cilantro stems.
Garnish with cilantro leaves, chili powder, and chili rings.
Heat oil in another pan until very hot, then drizzle the hot oil over the dish to finish.

mon_an.ten: Szechuan Poached Pork Slices (Shui Zhu Rou Pian)
mon_an.mo_ta: Szechuan Poached Pork Slices is a classic Szechuan dish featuring numbing spiciness and fresh aromas, with tender meat slices and crisp vegetables—perfect with rice. Pork tenderloin provides high-quality protein, combined with bean sprouts and other vegetables for balanced nutrition. The method is slightly detailed, requiring patience to marinate the meat and prepare the hand-chopped chilies; beginners will need about 1 to 2 hours to complete.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: 20g pickled red chilies (choose 0-40g depending on spice tolerance)
280g vegetable oil (adjust as needed; add 100g more for a richer oil finish)
200g rapeseed oil (adjust as needed; add 100g more for a richer oil finish)
20g dried bird's eye chilies (choose 0-40g depending on spice tolerance)
5g green Szechuan peppercorns (add 5g more for extra numbness)
cac_buoc: Cut the pork tenderloin into small pieces, then slice thinly to 2mm (adjust to taste). Place in a bowl, wash twice with clean water to remove blood and impurities, then drain and set aside.
Add 1.5g salt, 1g pepper powder, 5g light soy sauce, and 3g cooking wine to the bowl; stir in one direction for 2 minutes to infuse the flavors.

Prepare another bowl, add one egg white and 7g potato starch; stir in one direction. Pour this over the meat and stir again in one direction (this forms a smooth coating to keep the meat tender). Finally, add 30g vegetable oil and stir gently (to prevent slices from sticking).
Prepare 100g mung bean sprouts, 1 celtuce (cut into small strips), 3 stalks celery (cut into short segments), and 2 leeks (crushed and cut into segments).
Finely mince 20g garlic, a small piece of ginger, and 20g pickled red chilies.

Add 15g dried bird's eye chilies and 3g green Szechuan peppercorns to a pan. Heat slightly, then pour out excess oil, leaving about 50g in the pan. Add the dried chilies and peppercorns, stir-fry on low heat until fragrant (do not burn; they should turn dark), then remove and finely chop on a cutting board.

Heat the pan, add 100g vegetable oil until 60% hot. Add 2g green Szechuan peppercorns and dried chilies to infuse the oil. Add the side vegetables and 1g salt, stir-fry until just cooked, then place in the bottom of a serving bowl and set aside.

Clean the pan, add 150g vegetable oil until 60% hot. Add the prepared ginger, garlic, and pickled chilies. Sauté until fragrant, then add 10g Doubanjiang. Stir-fry on low heat until the red oil is released.

Add 800ml clean water (adjust as needed), bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to low heat to season. Add 2.5g salt, 1.5g chicken bouillon powder, 1g white sugar to enhance freshness, 1g pepper powder, and 5g starch slurry (adjust as needed) to slightly thicken the sauce.

While the water is simmering, add the marinated pork slices one by one on low heat. Switch to medium heat to poach the meat, using a spatula to gently push them to avoid sticking. Once the water boils and the meat is cooked, remove and place on top of the vegetables, then pour in the broth (do not submerge completely).
Evenly sprinkle the hand-chopped chilies, minced garlic, and chopped scallions over the bowl.
Clean the pan, add 200g rapeseed oil, heat until 70% hot, then drizzle evenly over the pork slices in the bowl (be careful of splashes). The dish is ready.
Vegetables for the base can be chosen to taste (mushrooms, napa cabbage, romaine lettuce, etc.).
If hand-chopping chilies is too much work, you can use whole dried chili segments and green peppercorns directly.
Pay special attention to marinating the meat (stir in one direction and remove blood water) to ensure a smooth, tender texture (egg white and starch mixture).
Szechuan Poached Beef can also be made using this method.

mon_an.mo_ta: This is a simple home-style stir-fry with a savory-sweet balance and a rich sauce aroma. The softened onions provide a mild sweetness that pairs perfectly with tender pork slices—a great dish for rice. Pork provides high-quality protein and B vitamins, while onions offer fiber and antioxidants to aid digestion. The process is simple and beginner-friendly, with an estimated cooking time of just 15 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: 1 onion (the main ingredient; use half to one full onion depending on preference)
Note: Consider using measuring spoons (tsp, tbsp) for accurate ingredient quantities.
cac_buoc: Slice the onion, prep the pork, crush the garlic, and mix the seasonings above; set aside.
Add 1 tbsp of cooking oil to the wok (wait 10 seconds for the oil to heat up), then add the pork.
Stir-fry until the meat changes color, add the garlic until fragrant, then remove and set aside.
Add the onions to the same pan and stir-fry for 3-4 minutes, then pour in the seasoning and mix well.
Return the set-aside pork to the pan and stir-fry until the meat is fully cooked.
Once the meat is cooked, stir-fry for another 1-2 minutes, then serve.
You can use sliced pork shoulder or pre-cut pork strips according to your preference.

mon_an.mo_ta: This is a specialty barbecue from Zibo, Shandong. The unique way of eating involves wrapping grilled meat in small pancakes with large scallions, creating a rich harmony of meat, sauce, and onion flavors. Pork belly provides protein and fat, while large scallions provide fiber, and the pancakes offer a quick energy boost. It requires control over charcoal heat and flipping techniques, which may be challenging for beginners; the whole process takes about 40 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Quantities are per person; increase proportionally for more people.
cac_buoc: Cut the pork belly into cubes no thicker than 2cm and thread them onto skewers. (The pork belly can be marinated slightly beforehand for better flavor.)
Cut the large scallion into 5cm segments and set aside.
Dilute the sesame paste with 10ml warm water, mix well with the sweet bean sauce, and set aside (can be replaced with "sesame salt").
Light the charcoal and wait until it is **glowing red with no open flames** (about 15 minutes).
Arrange the pork belly skewers evenly on the grill; grill until the *bottom is golden brown and the fat is rendered*, then flip.
Continue grilling for 2-3 minutes until *both sides are golden brown and the edges are slightly charred*, then remove from the heat.
Lay a small thin pancake flat and spread 3-4g of the sauce mixture on it.
Place the grilled meat and 1-2 scallion segments on top, roll it up, and enjoy.
When cutting the pork belly, it is recommended to freeze it for 30 minutes first to make it easier to slice.
Charcoal grilling provides better flavor than gas; use wood charcoal if possible.
The ratio of sesame paste to sweet bean sauce can be adjusted to taste, or replaced with sesame salt.

mon_an.mo_ta: Steamed Mandarin fish features tender meat and a prominent natural sweetness, representing a home-style river fish preparation that focuses on original flavors. Mandarin fish is rich in high-quality protein and micronutrients, making it easy to digest. Be careful with the fish fins during prep, but the overall steps are not complex and manageable for beginners. From prep to serving takes only about half an hour.
cac_buoc: **Prepare the ingredients**: Clean the Mandarin fish by removing the gills and innards, descaling, and scraping the slime off the skin (you can ask the fishmonger to do this). Score the body of the fish, place ginger slices on it, and if possible, add a little lard. Arrange on a plate with a pair of chopsticks underneath to ensure even heat distribution during steaming. Split the large scallion, remove the core, and keep the outer layers. Split the regular scallions and set aside. Deseed the red chili and remove the inner flesh. Stack the large scallion, regular scallions, and chili together, julienne finely, and soak in water; set aside.

**Steaming process**: Add water to a steamer (use a generous amount). When the water is boiling, place the fish inside, cover, and steam on high heat for 8-10 minutes. The secret to steaming fish is: high steam and high heat. While the fish is steaming, heat oil in another pan until it starts to smoke. After steaming, discard the liquid from the plate, remove the ginger slices, place the julienned aromatics on top, and drizzle with the hot oil. Pour light soy sauce or seasoned seafood soy sauce over the fish and serve.
**Notes**:
1. The dorsal fins of Mandarin fish are sharp; be careful during prep or cut them off with scissors.
2. Adjust steaming time based on the size of the fish; the key is plenty of water, high steam, and high heat.

mon_an.mo_ta: Hunan Home-style Braised Pork is a soul-satisfying dish where pork belly is slow-simmered until tender and melt-in-your-mouth without being greasy. It features a savory aroma with a hint of spice and a sweet finish. Rich in protein and fat, it provides ample energy. It requires patience and is slightly challenging for beginners, but following the steps makes it manageable; the process takes about 1 hour.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: One serving is enough for 2 people.
cac_buoc: Wash the pork belly (skin on), place in a pot of cold water with 2-3 slices of ginger to remove odors. Bring to a boil, then remove and rinse with cold water to clean off the foam.
Cut the pork belly into 1.5cm*1.5cm cubes.
Heat the pan with oil, add rock sugar, and stir over low heat until it turns a caramel color. Add the pork cubes and stir-fry over medium heat until evenly coated with color.

Add the prepared ginger slices, star anise, cinnamon, light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, cooking wine, dried bird's eye chilies, and salt. Stir-fry on low heat for 1 minute, then add boiling water until the meat is submerged.
Cover, bring to a boil over medium heat, then reduce to low heat and simmer for 30 minutes. Stir every 10 minutes to prevent sticking.
When the sauce has reduced to about one-third, switch to medium heat to reduce the sauce further until thickened, then serve.

mon_an.ten: Xiangqi Steamed Duck with Rice Flour
mon_an.mo_ta: A traditional specialty from the Liangqi region of Hunan: duck meat is stir-fried and then coated in a rice flour mixture before being steamed until tender, savory, and deeply flavorful. Duck is rich in protein and B vitamins, while the rice flour provides energy for a balanced meal. This requires pre-frying and then pressure cooking, making it suitable for those with some cooking experience. Takes about 1 hour; older ducks require longer steaming.
cac_buoc: Mix the glutinous rice flour, rice flour, steamed meat powder, chili powder, 5g salt, and white pepper powder together.
Have the duck chopped into bite-sized pieces for steaming. Slice the ginger, peel the garlic, and slice the pork belly.
Heat the pan and add oil; stir-fry the pork belly until the fat is rendered. Add more oil if needed, heat up, then add the duck.
Stir-fry the duck until the skin is browned, then add the ginger, garlic, and salt; continue stir-frying until fragrant.
Turn to low heat, pour in the rice flour mixture and toss so the duck is evenly coated. Add boiling water gradually in small batches while tossing.
Toss until the duck and flour feel moist, then transfer to a bowl. Place in a pressure cooker with water and steam for 20-25 minutes.
Garnish with chopped scallions before serving.
This is a traditional hometown dish.
Any type of duck works; here we used water duck.
Steam for 20 minutes; if using an old duck, steam for over an hour.
In step one, rice flour is the base, glutinous rice flour adds chewiness, steamed meat powder adds five-spice aroma, and chili/pepper add complexity.

mon_an.mo_ta: This is a classic Macanese-Portuguese fast-food dish. The savory minced beef is tender and coated in a rich gravy, topped with a soft-boiled egg that makes the rice glossy and irresistible when mixed. Minced beef provides high-quality protein, and combined with egg and onion, it is a balanced and filling meal. The steps are simple and beginner-friendly; takes about 30 minutes from prep to serving.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine the number of servings before starting. One serving is enough for 1 person.
1 egg (for poaching or a sunny-side-up egg with a runny yolk)
3 tbsp light soy sauce (1 tbsp for marinating, 2 tbsp for the sauce)
cac_buoc: Place 200g minced beef in a bowl, add 1 tbsp light soy sauce, half tbsp white sugar, and 2g black pepper. Mix well and **marinate for 10 minutes**.
Finely dice half an onion and set aside.
Prepare the sauce: in a bowl, mix 2 tbsp light soy sauce, 2 tbsp ketchup, 1 tbsp cooking wine, 1 tbsp starch, half tbsp dark soy sauce, and 50ml clean water; set aside.
In a separate pot, prepare a poached egg or a sunny-side-up egg with a runny yolk; set aside.
Heat a pan and add 10g butter. Once melted, add the diced onion and fry on low heat until cooked and fragrant.
Add the marinated minced beef and stir-fry with the onions until the beef changes color.
Pour in the prepared sauce, sprinkle with 2g black pepper, and continue stir-frying until the sauce thickens, then turn off the heat.
Pour the stir-fried beef over hot rice and top with the prepared egg.
(Optional) Garnish with 5g chopped scallions.
If you don't have butter, regular cooking oil works, but butter adds a unique milky aroma.
When eating, break the egg yolk and mix it thoroughly with the beef and rice for the best flavor.

mon_an.mo_ta: Mid-joint chicken wings are marinated until flavorful and roasted at high heat until the skin is slightly charred and the inside is tender and juicy, carrying the savory aroma of black pepper and soy sauce. Rich in protein and collagen. Moderate difficulty, easy for beginners; takes about 1 hour from prep to oven. Honey or five-spice powder can be added to enhance the flavor.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Calculate the total ingredients based on these ratios.
cac_buoc: Prep the chicken wings.
Place the wings in a bowl.
Add salt, black pepper, soy sauce, and cooking wine; marinate for 30-40 minutes.
Roasting process.
Preheat the oven to 200°C.
Arrange the marinated wings evenly on a baking tray.
Place the tray on the middle rack of the oven and roast for 15-20 minutes.
Remove the tray, flip the wings, and roast for another 15-20 minutes until fully cooked.
When marinating, you can add honey, soy sauce, ginger/garlic powder, or five-spice powder to enhance the taste and aroma.
It is recommended to line the baking tray with aluminum foil for easier cleanup.

mon_an.mo_ta: Crispy on the outside and tender on the inside with a rich aroma. The chops are first simmered with aromatics and then pan-seared to create a golden, crispy crust. The flavor is bold but not greasy, making it a perfect main dish for family meals or guests. Lamb is rich in protein and minerals like iron and zinc. While there are several steps, it is manageable for beginners; takes about 1 hour with a pressure cooker or 1.5 hours with a regular pot.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine the number of servings before starting. One serving is enough for 3-4 people.
25g salt (Note: if you plan to drink the lamb broth, omit salt during simmering and add it during the searing step)
cac_buoc: Chop the lamb chops into pieces following the bone structure.
Place the lamb in a wok with cold water. Bring to a boil and blanch for 2-3 minutes, then remove and set aside.
Place the blanched lamb, cinnamon, Szechuan peppercorns, star anise, Angelica dahurica, bay leaves, and cooking wine into a pot (pressure cooker or regular pot).
Add enough water to submerge all ingredients. If using a pressure cooker, cook for 30 minutes after it reaches pressure. If using a regular pot, simmer for 80 minutes.
Remove the simmered lamb chops and drain well. Place them in a dry wok or frying pan (no oil or water needed).
Sear over medium-high heat for 6-7 minutes until the lamb fat is rendered and the *surface is golden and crispy*.
Keep the rendered lamb fat in the pan, add the chili powder, cumin seeds, BBQ rub, cumin powder, and sesame seeds; stir-fry until fragrant.
Add the sugar and salt (if not added during simmering) and toss well.
Once evenly coated, turn off the heat and serve on a plate.
Szechuan peppercorns and Angelica dahurica are key spices for this dish; do not skip them.
Do not simmer for too long; if the lamb is too soft, it will fall apart during searing.
Utilize the rendered fat from the lamb itself to toast the spices for better flavor.
A lot of lamb fat is produced during blanching, simmering, and searing; please do not pour it directly down the drain to avoid clogging.

mon_an.mo_ta: This is a classic Western-style pan-seared steak with a fragrant, charred crust and a tender, juicy interior. Enhanced with butter, garlic, and herbs, it offers a rich and savory flavor. It is high in quality protein, healthy fats, and minerals like iron and zinc. The cooking process is beginner-friendly, though mastering the heat requires some practice; the entire process takes about 15-30 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine the number of servings before starting. One serving is enough for 2 people.
Thyme 2g (if using fresh sprigs, use 3-6 sprigs, each about 10cm long)
cac_buoc: Prepare the ingredients

Remove the steak from the refrigerator to thaw. If the steak is frozen, transfer it to the chiller the night before and let it sit at room temperature for half an hour before cooking. **Do not** let the steak **soak in water or use heat to thaw**.
Wash the cherry tomatoes, baby potatoes, and button mushrooms; halve them and set aside.
Peel the garlic, keep 5-8 large cloves, and **crush** them with the flat side of a knife; set aside.

Pre-process the steak. For ribeye steak (see steak selection guide), use kitchen shears to cut vertically into the connective tissue in the center of the ribeye 1-2 times. This is because the "eye" (the connective tissue) of the ribeye shrinks significantly at high temperatures, deforming the steak and causing uneven cooking. For sirloin steak, if you dislike the fat cap on the edge, you can trim it off with a knife. Then, wrap the steak in paper towels and pat thoroughly dry until no visible water marks are left on the cutting board.

Cooking. Note: This process applies to steaks 2-3cm thick, cooked to medium or medium-well. If you prefer a different level of doneness, consider increasing or decreasing the initial searing time by 20-30%.
Turn the stove to high heat (see the heat power appendix) and add olive oil to the pan; heat the pan for 15-30 seconds.

Season the steak. Sprinkle sea salt and black pepper evenly over the entire surface of the steak, then use your hands to rub and press the seasoning into the meat as much as possible. Note: After seasoning, the steak **must be placed in the pan immediately; pre-marinating is not recommended**. This is because salt draws moisture out of the beef, affecting the sear and flavor.
Heat the pan until the oil is 60-80% hot (refer to oil temperature tips), then slowly place the steak into the pan, laying it away from you.
If using potatoes as a side dish, you can place them in a bowl and microwave for 10 minutes, or boil them in water for 3-5 minutes.
Sear one side for 1.5 minutes (this time applies to steaks about 2-3cm thick. If your steak is thinner, consider shortening to 1 minute. If thicker, increase to 2-2.5 minutes).
Flip and sear the other side for another 1.5 minutes. For sirloin and fillet steaks, use tongs or a spatula to stand the steak up and sear the edges for about 30 seconds.

Switch to medium heat, then **quickly add** the butter, garlic, and thyme in that order. Use a spatula to move the butter around until completely melted. Press the garlic under the steak to infuse the flavor.
**Tilt the pan** on the stove so all the oil pools to one side.

Place the aromatics and garlic on top of the steak, use a spoon to scoop the hot oil, and continuously baste the steak. Continue this for 30 seconds, then flip the steak and repeat for another 30 seconds. Observe the oil as you baste; if it bubbles and doesn't turn dark brown, the temperature is correct. If the steak wasn't dried properly, was thawed incorrectly, or was salted too early, water will appear in the pan, causing the steak to "boil" and lose flavor. If the oil bubbles excessively and turns dark brown, the heat is too high; remove the pan from the heat, wait a moment, then continue basting.
Place the steak on a cutting board, wrap it in foil, and let it rest for 5-10 minutes. This process (resting) uses the residual heat to finish cooking and lock in the juices.
Add the side dishes (potatoes, tomatoes, mushrooms) to the pan and fry over medium heat for 5 minutes.
Remove the steak from the foil and slice into 1.5cm wide strips; you can now observe the doneness of the beef.
Plate the side dishes and drizzle with the remaining pan oil or steak sauce (optional).
Heat Control
Searing steak is the art of heat control. Due to length constraints, only simple quantitative methods for judging heat power and related terms are listed here. See oil temperature tips for more.
For induction cooktops:
High heat: 1.8kW - 2.2kW.
Medium heat: 800W - 1.4kW.
Low heat: 200W - 600W.
For gas stoves:
High heat: Turn the gas valve to 70%-90% of maximum flow.
Medium heat: Turn the gas valve to 40%-60% of maximum flow.
Low heat: Turn the gas valve to 10%-30% of maximum flow.
About Seasoning

Steak seasoning does not strictly have to follow this guide. Generally, garlic, black pepper, and butter are essential, but if you dislike herbs like rosemary or thyme, feel free to try other steak seasonings. Many grilled seasoning salts are available on the market. Some even use a fusion method, frying sliced chili and garlic in olive oil to drizzle over the finished steak for a unique flavor.

mon_an.mo_ta: Pork Skin Aspic is a traditional cold dish often served during Lunar New Year in Northern China. It is crystal clear, with a smooth, chewy, and crunchy texture, making it an excellent snack for drinks. Pork skin is rich in collagen, which is beneficial for the skin. This dish is slightly difficult and requires patience to deodorize the skin and simmer it for a long time; the total time is approximately 24 hours.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Seasonings: salt 13g, MSG 10g, chicken powder 15g, light soy sauce 50ml, dark soy sauce 20ml, green onions 10g, green onions 10g, sliced ginger 20g
Spice bag: star anise 10g, Sichuan peppercorns 5g
cac_buoc: Cut the pork skin into small pieces no larger than 10cm. Soak in clean water for 12 hours, then place in a pot of cold water with 10g ginger and 50ml cooking wine. Blanch for 5-10 minutes, then remove and place in cold water.
Place the blanched pork skin on a cutting board, scrape off all the white fat from the inside, then cut into strips no wider than 3mm and place in a basin.
Add 20g white vinegar and 5g salt, scrub vigorously for 3 minutes, then rinse with clean water until the fishy smell is gone.

Add 4kg of water to a pot along with the pork skin, 10g green onions, 10g sliced ginger, 10g star anise, and 5g Sichuan peppercorns. Bring to a boil over high heat, then simmer over low heat for 90 minutes until the pork skin is very tender.

Add 8g salt, 10g MSG, 15g chicken powder, 50ml light soy sauce, and 20ml dark soy sauce to season. Pour into a dish, remove the green onions, ginger, and star anise, and let cool until it sets into a jelly.
Place in the refrigerator to chill. When serving, cut into small pieces or thick slices.

When making this, remember that putting the skin directly into the pot to cook is a mistake. You must use white vinegar and salt to scrub the skin repeatedly; this ensures the finished aspic is crystal clear and free of any odor.

mon_an.ten: Braised Pork with Pickled Mustard Greens
mon_an.mo_ta: Braised Pork with Pickled Mustard Greens is a Northern-style home-cooked stew. It is savory and aromatic, featuring tender pork belly and flavorful ribs. It provides high protein, and the pickled greens offer beneficial lactic acid bacteria. The steps are clear for beginners to follow, but it requires patience for slow simmering; the process takes about 3 hours from start to finish.
cac_buoc: Cut the large green onion into sections; cut 50g of ginger into sections and mince the remaining 50g; mince the garlic and set aside.

Shred all the pickled mustard greens and rinse with water 2-3 times; set aside. The number of rinses depends on your taste; rinse twice for a sourer flavor or 3-4 times if you prefer it milder. Do not skip rinsing, or it will be too sour.

Place the ribs and pork belly in a pot and cover with cold water. Add the green onion sections, 50g ginger sections, and 20ml cooking wine. Bring to a boil over high heat and wait for 5 minutes. Turn off the heat, remove the ribs and pork belly, rinse off the scum with cold water, and set aside.
Slice or cube the parboiled pork belly and set aside.
Wash and dry the pot used previously (to prevent oil from splashing).

Add oil to the pan over medium heat, sauté the minced ginger and garlic until fragrant, then add the pork belly and ribs. Fry until golden brown, then add 10g five-spice powder and 15g light soy sauce; stir-fry for 1-2 minutes.
Add the rinsed shredded pickled mustard greens to the pan and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Pour in enough purified water to just cover the ingredients, add 2 star anise, and switch to high heat until the water boils. Switch to medium heat, cover, and simmer.
Wait for 1.5-2 hours until the pork belly is tender (easily pierced with a chopstick).
Open the lid, turn to high heat to reduce the broth, stirring until the liquid only covers the bottom of the pan. Switch to low heat and prepare to season.
Seasoning: Add 10g salt and stir well.
Turn off the heat and serve.
When reducing the broth over high heat, be careful not to burn the pan; stir occasionally to check the water level.
Seasoning tip: Add the salt gradually at the end, stirring and tasting until the flavor is to your liking.
This dish has the unique, characteristic flavor of pickled mustard greens.

mon_an.ten: Sweet and Spicy Roasted Whole Chicken Wings
mon_an.mo_ta: These sweet and spicy whole chicken wings are made in an air fryer, resulting in a slightly charred skin and juicy interior. The sweet and spicy flavor profile is very popular. Chicken is rich in quality protein, and using an air fryer instead of deep-frying significantly reduces fat, making it a lighter meal. The process is straightforward, requiring only pre-marinating and flipping once halfway through, making it very beginner-friendly. It takes about 3 hours from preparation to serving, though most of that is passive marinating time.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: One serving is for one person; increase proportionally for more people.
cac_buoc: Take 4 fresh whole chicken wings and use a knife to score the skin between the two bones of the mid-wing, one cut on each side.

Place the 4 wings in a bowl and add 45ml light soy sauce, 15ml dark soy sauce, 10g garlic powder, 5g pepper powder, 10g sugar, 10g paprika, 5g chili powder, 15ml oyster sauce, 20ml water, and 10ml oil.
Use a spoon to coat the wings evenly with the sauce, especially in the scores on the mid-wings; this takes about 3 minutes.
Cover the bowl with plastic wrap to prevent odors and let marinate in the refrigerator for 120 minutes.
Remove the wings and place them in a foil tray; pour the remaining marinade from the bowl evenly over the wings.
Place the foil tray in the air fryer basket and roast at 200°C for 25 minutes.
Open the air fryer, carefully remove the foil tray, and flip the wings.
Continue roasting at 200°C for another 25 minutes.
Remove and serve.
The wings in this recipe are mildly spicy; to increase the heat, add more chili powder, but do not exceed 30g.
Whole chicken wings include the wing tip, mid-wing, and drumette.
The desired effect is a slight char; if you prefer a less browned look, do not pour the extra marinade into the tray and roast each side for only 20 minutes.
Actual roasting results should be judged based on your air fryer's power.
Paprika is used for color and flavor; it is not a source of heat.
Marinating time can be adjusted; 60 to 180 minutes is recommended.
The foil tray is very hot when it comes out; please use tongs, a wet towel, or similar heat protection to handle it.

mon_an.mo_ta: Stuffed Field Snails is the top of Yangshuo's "eighteen stuffed dishes." The snail meat is chewy and firm, the pork is smooth and tender, and the fresh perilla and mint provide a refreshing aroma. This dish was featured on "A Bite of China 2." It is rich in protein and micronutrients, with snail and pork complementing each other's nutrition. The steps are numerous and may challenge beginners; snails need to purge sand for half a day, and the active cooking time is about 40 minutes. It's a great family activity for holidays.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Light soy sauce 30ml (15ml for the filling, 15ml for the braising liquid)
cac_buoc: Purge the snails (half a day in advance).
Buy the snails in the morning, place them in a basin of clean water, and let them sit all afternoon to purge sand.
You can add a few drops of sesame oil (or mustard!) to the water to encourage purging. Process the snails.
Use a brush to scrub the snail shells clean (take your time with this step).
Use pliers or a knife to snip off the snail tails (about 1/3 to 1/2 of the shell).
Boil a large pot of water; once boiling, blanch the snails for 1-2 minutes (not too long, or the meat will become tough).
Remove and use a toothpick to extract the meat; discard the operculum (snail lid) and the black digestive tract.
Rinse the shells with water and shake dry; set aside. Make the filling.
Scrub the snail meat with salt, rinse, and mince into small bits (do not grind into a paste; keep some texture for chewiness).
Mince the pork.
Finely chop the mint, perilla, ginger, and green onions.
In a bowl, combine the minced snail meat, pork, mint, perilla, ginger, and green onions.
Add 15ml Sanhua liquor, 15ml light soy sauce, and 3g salt.
Optional: add 10ml oyster sauce, 2g white pepper powder, and 10g starch.
Stir in one direction until the filling is thick and sticky.
For convenience, all the above ingredients can be processed in a meat grinder. Stuffing.
Use chopsticks to stuff the filling into the snail shells; try to pack it tightly but do not break the shells.
Repeat until all snails are stuffed. Braising.
Heat a pan, pour in 30ml oil, and sauté the sour bamboo shoots and dried chilies until fragrant (optional).
Pour in about 300ml water or broth, add 15ml light soy sauce and 2g salt; bring to a boil over high heat.
Add the stuffed snails to the pan, cover, and simmer over medium-low heat for 10 minutes.
Do not stir frequently while braising; wait until the meat is 60-70% cooked and set before gently tossing.
Open the lid, add the remaining fresh mint and perilla, and simmer for another 2-3 minutes.
Turn to high heat to reduce the sauce until thickened, then serve.
How to eat: first suck the juices from the shell, then use a toothpick or suck hard to pull out the filling.
The best ratio of snail meat to pork is 1:1.
Mint is the essence of this dish, and perilla is the perfect match for snails; you must have at least one of them.
If Sanhua liquor is unavailable, use cooking wine, though the flavor will be slightly different.
Blanching time must be short; otherwise, the snail meat will become tough.
Pairing with a chilled Liquan beer is the authentic Yangshuo way to enjoy this dish.

mon_an.mo_ta: This Italian-style sauce is fragrant and savory, with a combination of vegetables and beef providing a rich depth of flavor. It is high in protein and vitamins, offering balanced nutrition. The process is somewhat detailed and requires some cooking basics, such as browning beef until crumbly and controlling the heat for a slow simmer. It takes about an hour from prep to finish; you can make a large batch and freeze it for convenient use later.
cac_buoc: Finely dice the carrot, celery, and onion; slice the garlic.
Add 10ml olive oil to a pan; when hot, sauté the vegetables over high heat. Once they start to change color, remove them from the pan.
Add another 10ml of oil to the pan, sauté the garlic for 10 seconds, then add the ground beef, sugar, salt, pepper, and seasonings. Sauté until the beef is browned and crumbly.
Add the sautéed vegetables and tomato sauce back into the pan and stir well.
Slowly pour in the milk in several batches. Simmer over medium-low heat for 30 minutes until finished.
**Since salt content varies between tomato sauce brands, it is recommended to use less salt when sautéing the beef, then taste and adjust at the end.**
**Please stir occasionally while simmering to prevent the sauce from sticking to the pan. Once the sauce has thickened, it is ready to serve!**
Depending on your preference, you can use a half-beef, half-pork mixture, or replace the milk with chicken broth or water.

mon_an.ten: Stir-Fried Lean Pork with Sliced Potatoes
mon_an.mo_ta: A quick home-style stir-fry: tender pork slices paired with soft yet chewy potatoes, infused with the fresh aroma of green garlic. This is a quintessential family dish. Lean pork provides high-quality protein and iron, while potatoes offer starch and fiber for a balanced meal. The process is simple and clear, requiring basic knife skills and heat control, making it suitable for beginners with some experience. It takes about 1 hour from prep to serving.
cac_buoc: Peel the potatoes, halve them, and cut into thin slices about 2mm thick; set aside.
Wash the green garlic and cut into 1cm sections; set aside.
Wash the lean pork and cut into thin slices about 2mm thick. Place in a bowl with 5g starch, 5g light soy sauce, and 3g dark soy sauce. Marinate for 10 minutes; set aside.
While the pork is marinating, bring a pot of water to a boil. Add the potato slices and blanch for about 5 minutes.
Heat a pan and add 10ml - 15ml of cooking oil. Wait 10 seconds for the oil to heat up.
Add the pork and stir-fry until it changes color, then add the green garlic and stir-fry for about 20 seconds.
Add the potatoes and continue to stir-fry. Add 2g salt and 5g light soy sauce.
Stir-fry for about 3 minutes, then serve.
When blanching the potatoes, be careful not to overcook them to prevent them from becoming too mushy.
Ensure the pork is stirred well with the marinade.

mon_an.ten: Braised Pork with Napa Cabbage and Glass Noodles
mon_an.mo_ta: This is a classic Northeastern Chinese home-style stew. The broth is rich and savory, the pork belly is melt-in-your-mouth tender, and the glass noodles soak up the meaty aroma while remaining smooth and chewy. The napa cabbage adds a refreshing sweetness that balances the richness. This all-in-one dish provides protein, vitamins, and starch. It requires some patience, especially with the noodles and simmering time, but following the steps ensures success. It takes about 45 minutes from start to finish.
cac_buoc: Bring water to a boil in a pot, add the dried glass noodles, and cook for 5 minutes. Pour the noodles and water into a container, cover, and continue soaking; set aside (do this first while preparing other steps).
Slice the pork belly into 3mm pieces; set aside.
Separate the napa cabbage leaves from the stems and cut both into slices; set aside.
Heat a pan and add 10ml - 15ml of cooking oil. Wait 10 seconds for the oil to heat up.
Add the pork belly and stir-fry continuously until it changes color.
Add the dark soy sauce and stir-fry for **1 minute** to color the meat.
Add the cabbage stems, salt, and light soy sauce; stir-fry for one minute (if it sticks to the pan, drizzle in 10ml of water).
Add enough water to cover the ingredients, then add the chicken powder and thirteen-spice powder. Once boiling, lower the heat and **wait for 20 minutes**.
Drain the glass noodles and cut into shorter sections; set aside in a bowl.
Add the cabbage leaves, stir well, then place the glass noodles on top of the vegetables. Cover and cook for another **5 minutes**.
Taste, turn off the heat, and reduce the sauce if necessary.
Dried potato glass noodles take a long time to cook, so start them first.
Taste at the final step; if the flavor is too light or the food isn't tender enough, cover and cook for a bit longer.

mon_an.mo_ta: Air fryer fried chicken is a home-style dish where chicken is marinated and then "fried" to achieve a crispy skin and juicy interior. The seasoning can be adjusted to your preference.
