Chicken wings provide quality protein and fats, making them a great main or snack. The active time is about 55-70 minutes (for single dredging; double dredging takes 70-90 minutes). For the best results, marinate overnight.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine the number of servings before starting. This recipe is for 1 serving (6 mid-wings, about 300g), which fits in a single layer in most air fryers.
cac_buoc: Marinate the chicken (the night before).
Wash the mid-wings and pat dry. Score each side of the wings twice to help the flavor penetrate.
Prepare the marinade: mix 15ml light soy sauce, 8g garlic powder, 5g paprika, 3g onion powder, 3g black pepper powder, and 5ml milk or Greek yogurt (optional, makes the meat more tender).
Place the marinade and wings in a large Ziploc bag, massage well, and let rest in the refrigerator overnight. Prepare the coating.
Flour coating: mix 60g all-purpose flour, 30g starch, 5g garlic powder, 5g paprika, 2g onion powder, 2g black pepper powder, and 1g baking powder (optional, for extra crispiness).
Egg wash (optional): whisk 1 egg with 5ml milk or water until smooth. Dredging.
Dredging: shake off excess moisture from the wings, press them into the flour coating, shake off the excess, and let rest for 10 minutes.

Double coating (optional): for a thicker crust, dip the rested wings into the egg wash, shake off the excess, then press into the flour coating again. Shake off excess and let rest for 20 minutes (longer if possible to help the crust set). Frying.
Preheat the air fryer to 180°C for 5 minutes.
Brush a thin layer of oil on the basket. Place the wings skin-side down and spray or brush a thin layer of oil on top.
Set the air fryer to 180°C and fry for 10 minutes.
Open the basket, flip the wings, spray or brush another thin layer of oil, and fry for 6 minutes at 180°C.
Observe the color of the skin and pierce the thickest part with a toothpick to check for clear juices.
If needed, fry for another 1-2 minutes at 200°C for extra crispiness and color (repeat in 1-minute increments if necessary).
This recipe can also be used for bone-in drumsticks; just adjust the quantities and cooking time accordingly.
Garlic powder, paprika, and onion powder can be adjusted to taste.
For a spicy version: add 3g chili powder to the flour coating or sprinkle 2g on top after cooking.
For a cumin version: sprinkle 2g cumin powder and 2g white sesame seeds after cooking.
Do not stack the wings; this prevents even heat distribution and results in a less crispy crust.

mon_an.ten: Steamed Pork with Rice Flour (Phấn chưng nhục)
mon_an.mo_ta: Steamed Pork with Rice Flour is a classic Chinese steamed dish known for its rich aroma and soft, sticky texture. It is a widely loved home-style flavor. Pork belly provides quality protein and fat, while the base of root vegetables like potatoes ensures a balanced meal. This dish is suitable for those with some cooking experience and takes about 90 minutes from prep to finish.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine the number of servings before starting. One serving is enough for 3 people.
cac_buoc: Wash the pork belly and cut into slices about 5cm long, 3cm wide, and 0.5cm thick.
Finely mince the ginger and garlic into pieces no larger than 1mm.
In a large bowl, combine the sliced pork belly, 15ml light soy sauce, 10ml dark soy sauce, 15ml cooking wine, 10g broad bean paste, 10g minced ginger, 10g minced garlic, and 5g sugar.
Stir well with chopsticks, cover with plastic wrap, and marinate for 30 minutes at room temperature (20°C - 25°C).
After marinating, add 100g toasted rice powder and mix for 2 minutes, ensuring every slice of meat is evenly coated.
Peel the potatoes and cut into slices 0.8cm thick, about 5cm x 5cm in size, weighing about 300g in total.
Line the bottom of a 20cm deep bowl with the potato slices, trying not to overlap them too much.
Layer the coated pork belly evenly over the potatoes and press down firmly.
Add 2000ml of water to a steamer and bring to a rolling boil (100°C).
Place the bowl in the steamer and cover.
Steam over medium heat for 60 minutes (maintain a steady boil, approximately 600W).
When the time is up, pierce the center of a meat slice with a chopstick; if it goes through easily with no resistance, it is done.
If not yet tender, continue steaming for another 10-15 minutes until the meat is melt-in-your-mouth soft and the fat has rendered.
Remove and serve.

To make your own rice powder: toast 150g of rice in a pan over medium-low heat until slightly golden (about 8 minutes). Add 1g dried chili, 1g Sichuan peppercorns, and 0.5g star anise; toast until fragrant, then grind into a coarse powder and sift.
During steaming, if the water level drops below 1cm, immediately add 500ml of hot water (above 90°C) to maintain sufficient steam.

mon_an.mo_ta: Sweet and Sour Pork Ribs is a famous traditional dish known for its delicious sweet and tangy flavor, crispy exterior, and tender interior. Ribs are rich in high-quality protein and calcium, offering excellent nutritional benefits. This recipe involves several techniques such as blanching, frying, caramelizing sugar, and reducing the sauce. It requires a certain level of control over heat and seasoning, making it slightly challenging for beginners, but following this optimized process ensures a high success rate. Estimated cooking time is about 45 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Cooking oil 300–350 ml (adjust based on pan size; if deep-frying, use enough to cover 2/3 of the ribs)
cac_buoc: Place the ribs and ginger slices in cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat until plenty of foam appears, then switch to medium heat. Once boiling steadily, turn to low heat and blanch for 2–3 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Rinse the ribs 2–3 times with boiling water to ensure all blood foam is completely removed.

Pour enough oil into a pan for deep-frying (amount depends on pan size, approximately 300 ml for a standard household). When the oil temperature reaches about 170°C, add the ribs and fry for 3–5 minutes until the surface is slightly golden. Remove and drain.

Take another clean pan, place over low heat, and add 50 ml of hot water. Add 30 g of white granulated sugar and stir gently until the sugar is completely dissolved and turns a pale yellow. The focus of this step is observing the sugar's dissolution rather than relying solely on color changes.

Add the fried ribs to the sugar syrup and toss quickly for 30 seconds. Then add 5 ml aromatic vinegar, 5 ml light soy sauce, 5 ml oyster sauce, 2 g chicken bouillon powder, 10 g ketchup, and 0.5 g five-spice powder. Toss for another 30 seconds to coat the ribs evenly, then add enough boiling water to just cover the ribs.

Bring to a boil over high heat. Add 5 ml dark soy sauce for color and quickly reduce the sauce. If the rib pieces are large, you can switch to low heat and braise for 5–10 minutes to deepen the flavor, but do not simmer on medium heat for 20 minutes as it may ruin the texture.
Remove from the pot and serve on a plate. Sprinkle with 2 g of sesame seeds and enjoy.
When frying the ribs, you can lightly dust them with dry starch to increase crispiness if desired.

Pay attention to heat adjustments during blanching: start with cold water on high heat until boiling and foamy, then switch to medium, and finally low heat. Always rinse with boiling water after blanching to prevent the meat from drying out due to temperature shock.
The key to step four is ensuring the white sugar is completely dissolved; do not rely strictly on color to judge.
Stir quickly while reducing the sauce so the ribs are evenly coated, and avoid over-braising which can spoil the taste.

mon_an.mo_ta: Sweet and Sour Pork Tenderloin features a bold sweet and tangy flavor with a crispy crust and tender meat. It is a beloved family favorite found in many regional cuisines. While pork tenderloin provides high-quality protein, the batter and sweet and sour sauce make it relatively high in calories. Success depends on mastering the marinade, the double-fry technique, and sauce consistency. It can be challenging for beginners, so it is recommended to prepare all ingredients beforehand. Total time from prep to serving is about 45 minutes to 1 hour.
cac_buoc: Marinate the meat: Slice the tenderloin into thick pieces first, then lightly pound with the back of a knife to tenderize. Cut into finger-sized strips. Add cooking wine, light soy sauce, oyster sauce, salt, white pepper powder, and one egg. Mix well by hand and marinate for at least 20 minutes.
Prepare the sauce: Mix ketchup + 10g vinegar + 30g sugar + 150ml water. Stir until the sugar dissolves and set aside.
Coat with starch: Coat all the meat strips before you start frying to avoid rushing. Prepare a large bowl with starch and dredge each strip until fully covered.
Fry: Heat oil to 160°C. You can test the oil by inserting a dry chopstick; if small bubbles form around it, it is ready. Add the pork.

Fry until the surface is pale yellow, then remove. Maintain medium heat throughout. Wait for the oil temperature to rise to 200°C, then return the pork to the pan for a second fry. This only takes 40 seconds to make the crust very crispy. Remove immediately.
Coat with sauce: In a separate pan, add a little base oil. Pour in the prepared sauce and cook until it bubbles. Add the fried pork and stir-fry so each strip is coated in sauce.
Toss the fried pork quickly in the sauce, then turn off the heat and serve.
The pork must be fried in stages; pay close attention to the heat to achieve the perfect crispy-outside, tender-inside texture!

mon_an.mo_ta: Braised Pork Trotters is a classic home-style dish with a rich sauce and tender, chewy meat that is savory, fragrant, and slightly sweet—perfect with rice. Trotters are rich in collagen and protein. This dish is a bit challenging for beginners, but using a pressure cooker simplifies the process. It is easier for those with some cooking experience. Total time from prep to finish is about 1 hour.
cac_buoc: Getting started
Place the pork trotters (pre-chopped by the butcher) into a pot of cold water. Add 20 ml of cooking wine, green onion, and ginger. Cook for 15 minutes to remove the raw blood scent.
Heat the pan then add 30ml of oil. Add 7–8 pieces of rock sugar and turn to low heat to make a caramel. Crush the rock sugar with a spatula while stirring for about 2 minutes.
Once the caramel is ready, add the blanched trotters. Keep the heat low and stir-fry until both sides of the trotters are slightly golden.

Add 2 bay leaves, 1 cinnamon stick, 4 star anise, 20 ml light soy sauce, 20 ml dark soy sauce, 10 ml cooking wine, 3 slices of ginger, and 8 grams of salt. Switch to medium heat and stir-fry for 1 minute.
Add boiling or cold water until the trotters are submerged. Cover, bring to a boil over high heat, then turn off the stove.
Transfer everything from the pan into a pressure cooker. Cook for 15 minutes (if you don't have a pressure cooker, you can simmer in the pan over low heat until tender).
After 15 minutes, pour the contents back into a wok or pan. Turn to high heat to reduce the sauce. Taste at this point; if it's too light, add 2–3g of salt.
The reduction time on high heat depends on the amount of liquid, usually 30 seconds is enough. It's fine to leave a bit of extra sauce as it goes very well with rice.

mon_an.mo_ta: This braised pork belly features a glossy red finish, fat that melts in your mouth, and lean meat that is tender without being dry. It has the characteristic sweet-savory profile of Southern Chinese cuisine. Pork belly provides high-quality protein and collagen, while the aromatic spices remove gaminess and provide warmth. Although it requires caramelizing sugar and slow simmering, the steps are clearly broken down for beginners. The entire process takes about 1.5 hours.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: One portion serves 2-3 people (for 1 person, halve all quantities).
Pork belly: 1000g (approx. 2 lbs). *Note: Raw meat shrinks and loses fat during cooking; this amount yields enough for 2-3 people. For 1 person, halve all ingredients.*
Oil: 100-150ml (salad oil, lard, or peanut oil)
Green onion: approx. 30g (3-4 stalks), white parts cut into sections and set aside
Garlic: approx. 25g (5-6 cloves), halved and set aside
Rock sugar: 50g (approx. 15 thumb-sized pieces). If 50g was already used for caramelizing, this 50g is for seasoning during simmering; adjust to 30g if you prefer it less sweet.
Cooking wine: 30ml total (20ml for blanching, 10ml for simmering)
Cold water: enough to cover ingredients, depending on pan size
Boiling water: enough to cover ingredients, depending on pan size
cac_buoc: It is recommended to review the sugar caramelization guide first.
Keep the `pork belly` in large chunks that fit in the pan (about 5–6cm wide).
Slice the `fresh ginger` (each slice about 3mm thick).
Bring `boiling water` to a boil.
Use `cold water` from the tap.
Cut the `white parts` of the green onions into short sections.
Halve the `garlic` cloves; do not crush them, or they will be hard to remove and affect the texture during the `sauce reduction` phase.

Divide the aromatics into two preparation bowls: **Prep A (for blanching)**: 2 ginger slices, 2 onion sections. **Prep B (for simmering)**: Remaining 4 ginger slices, white onion sections, garlic cloves, Sichuan peppercorns, star anise, and bay leaves. Set aside.
Place the large pork belly chunks in a pot of cold water. Add **20ml cooking wine** and **Prep A**. Cook for 15 minutes to remove blood and odors, then rinse clean.

Remove the blanched pork and let it cool slightly. Cut into cubes approximately **3cm × 3cm × 3cm**. (Blanching firms the meat, making it easier to cut uniform cubes than raw meat. A 3cm raw cube results in a perfect 2.5cm bite-sized finished piece).

In a separate pan, caramelize the sugar. Note: **Use 'Method 2' from the guide**: when the sugar water forms thick bubbles, quickly add **Prep B** (ginger, onion whites, garlic, peppercorns, star anise, bay leaves) to fry until fragrant.

Once fragrant (about 5-10 seconds), **do not add water yet**. Immediately add the blanched `pork belly` and stir-fry over `high heat` to coat with color and render some fat. When it smells fragrant, pour in boiling water to fully submerge the meat. Cover and simmer over medium-low heat for 50-60 minutes (40 minutes for a pressure cooker).
Add **10ml cooking wine**.
Cover and bring to a boil. Every 25 minutes, open the lid to skim off fat and foam from the surface.
When the water level drops to about 3/5 of the meat's height, switch to medium heat. Remove all aromatics except the meat and liquid, and begin reducing the sauce.
With the lid off, when the sauce is almost gone and becomes thick and syrupy, remove from the heat (do not let it dry out completely).

mon_an.mo_ta: This appetizing home-style dish is glossy red, tender, rich but not greasy, and full of savory soy flavor—perfect with steamed rice. Pork belly provides high-quality protein and essential fatty acids. Adding quail eggs or dried bean curd skin makes it even more nutritious. The method is beginner-friendly, taking about 1.5 hours from prep to serving.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine the number of servings before starting. One portion serves 2-3 people.
If cooking for 1 person, consider halving the ingredients.
Boiling water: enough to cover ingredients, approx. 600ml-900ml
Quail eggs (optional, can substitute with chicken eggs): 0-2 eggs
cac_buoc: Prepare ingredients
Cut the `pork belly` into large cubes (approx. 4.5cm; freezing for 30-60 mins makes it easier to cut).
Cut the `dried bean curd skin` into 2cm wide strips.
Slice the `fresh ginger` (approx. 3mm thick).
Bring `water` to a boil.
Boil the `quail eggs`, peel them, and prick them with a `fork` or `toothpick` (make several holes so they absorb the flavor).
Prepare the `white parts` of the large green onions. Getting started
Place the cut `pork belly` into a pot of cold water with cooking wine, green onion, and ginger. Cook for 15 minutes to remove blood and odors.
Add two slices of `fresh ginger` to enhance the flavor.
Turn the heat to medium-low and place the `pork belly` directly into the pan without oil. Sear all six sides of each cube until the fat starts to render.
Pour off the rendered fat and set aside. Push the `pork belly` to one side, add 15g of `rock sugar`, and stir until melted.
Once melted, toss the pork with the sugar until well-coated and colored. Add 10ml `light soy sauce`, 15ml `dark soy sauce`, and 5ml `cooking wine`. Stir-fry until the color deepens.
Pour in the `boiling water` and simmer for 40 minutes (if you cut the pieces very large, extend the simmering time). Add 2 slices of `fresh ginger`, 3 `bay leaves`, and 2 `star anise` pieces.
Cover and bring to a boil. Add the boiled, pricked `quail eggs` and `dried bean curd skin`. Simmer over medium-low heat for 40 minutes. (Stir occasionally to prevent sticking).
Open the lid. When the sauce is nearly gone, turn to high heat to reduce the sauce (do not let it dry out completely).
Add 2-3g of `salt`, toss briefly, and serve.

mon_an.mo_ta: Braised Chicken Wings is a savory-sweet household favorite. They have a glossy red color and tender meat that easily falls off the bone. Chicken wings are rich in high-quality protein and collagen. The difficulty is moderate; beginners can master it by following the steps. Total time from prep to serving is about 40 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine servings before starting; one portion serves 3-4 people.
Dried chilies 2 pieces (optional, approx. 5g; omit if you don't like spice)
cac_buoc: Wash the chicken wings. Make three diagonal cuts on the thick part of the wing and one prick on the back to help the flavor penetrate.
If the wings are not very fresh, soak them in ginger water for 10-20 minutes after scoring.

Prepare 10g ginger slices (3-4 slices), 15g green onion sections (2-3 pieces); lightly crush 3-4 garlic cloves (approx. 15g) with a knife (no need to mince). Set aside 1 bay leaf, 1 star anise, and 2 dried chilies (optional).
Place the wings in a pot of cold water. Add 20ml of cooking wine and 2 slices of ginger (approx. 5g). Bring to a boil over high heat. Once boiling, cook for 2-3 minutes and skim off the foam.
Remove the wings and rinse twice with warm water to remove all blood foam. Drain and set aside.
Heat another pan and add 10-15ml of cooking oil.

When the oil is 50% hot, add 15g rock sugar. Use high heat to melt the sugar. Once it melts and changes color, switch to low heat. Continue stirring until it turns a deep apple-red color. Immediately add the drained wings and stir-fry quickly for 1-2 minutes until evenly coated in color.
Add the bay leaf, star anise, dried chilies (optional), remaining 2 ginger slices (5g), 15g green onion sections, and crushed garlic. Stir-fry for 30 seconds until the spices are fragrant.
Pour 15ml cooking wine and 15ml light soy sauce around the edges of the pan. Stir-fry quickly for 10 seconds.
Add warm water (approx. 50-60°C) until the wings are just submerged.
Add 5ml dark soy sauce, 3g salt, 2g white sugar, and 1g pepper powder. Stir gently with a spoon to combine.
Cover and cook over medium heat for 7-8 minutes.
Open the lid and use chopsticks to remove and discard the bay leaf, star anise, ginger, onion sections, and garlic.
Switch to high heat and stir constantly until the sauce thickens into a glaze (about 1-2 minutes).
Turn off the heat, plate the wings, and drizzle the remaining thick sauce over them.
Finally, garnish with 3g white sesame seeds and 5g chopped green onions. Done.
If there is any remaining gamey smell, you can double the amount of aromatic spices.

mon_an.mo_ta: Braised Lamb Chops with Noodles is a hearty Northern Chinese home-style dish. The lamb is tender and fragrant, while the wide noodles soak up the rich sauce for a satisfying bite. This all-in-one meal provides protein, starch, and essential fats. The process involves stewing the lamb and hand-kneading the dough, making it suitable for those with some cooking experience. The entire process takes about 1.5 hours.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Green peppers and bell peppers, 2 each
cac_buoc: Place the lamb in a pot of cold water to blanch. Once boiling, skim off the foam and remove the lamb.
Slice fresh ginger (4 slices). Place dried chilies and Sichuan peppercorns in a bowl and set aside.
Add oil to a wok. (A generous amount is fine.)
When the oil is hot, add white sugar and stir-fry the lamb until it develops a caramel color.
Once the moisture from the lamb has evaporated, add salt, dark soy sauce, and the prepared spices.
Add enough fresh water to submerge the lamb. Bring to a boil over high heat and cook for 10 minutes, then simmer over low heat for 30 minutes.
While the lamb is simmering, prepare the dough. Flour quantities and methods are explained in the supplementary section *(Note 1)*.
Add the green peppers, bell peppers, large green onions, and the hand-pulled dough pieces to the pan.
Toss everything together and serve. *Note 1: Store-bought noodles can be used as a substitute, but try to choose wide noodles.
(Dough Preparation - Ingredients)
All-purpose flour 300 g
Salt 3 g
Water 180 ml
(Dough Preparation - Method)
Mix ingredients, adding water gradually while stirring, then knead into a smooth dough.
Rest the dough (10 minutes).
Knead again until smooth.
Rest the dough (5 minutes).
Roll the dough into a long log and cut into 6 to 8 small pieces.
Brush with oil and wait 5 minutes.
Roll each piece into a flat sheet.
Add to the braising pot and cook for 4 minutes (add one piece at a time).

mon_an.mo_ta: Mother's Style Stewed Pork Trotters features a milky white broth and trotters so tender they fall off the bone. The texture is smooth and rich, served with a spicy and sour dipping sauce that is very appetizing. This is a classic Sichuan home-style dish. Trotters are rich in collagen, and white kidney beans add a creamy, nutty texture. This recipe requires a pressure cooker and pre-soaking, which may be challenging for beginners. Including soaking and pressure cooking, the process takes about 2 hours (excluding overnight bean soaking).
cac_buoc: Getting started
Soak 200g of white kidney beans in water overnight and set aside.
Prepare the front trotters. Ask the butcher to split them down the middle. Use a torch to singe off any hair, then wash thoroughly at home.
Place the trotters, green onion sections, ginger slices, and cooking wine in a pot of cold water. Blanch for ten minutes, skim off the foam, then rinse and set aside.

Place the trotters, angelica root, dahurian angelica (bạch chỉ), white pepper powder, and ginger slices in a pressure cooker. Once it reaches pressure, cook for thirty minutes. Add the white kidney beans and pressure cook for another ten minutes. If the broth is milky white, you have succeeded (if you need to add water at any point, use only hot water).
After releasing the pressure, season with salt, chicken bouillon powder, and chopped green onions.

Prepare the 'soul' dipping sauce: combine green onions, garlic, bird's eye chilies, white pepper powder, light soy sauce, aromatic vinegar, hot chili oil, Sichuan pepper oil, and a splash of the trotter broth.
Drizzle the 'soul' dipping sauce over the meat or serve on the side.

mon_an.ten: Old-School Crispy Sweet and Sour Pork
mon_an.mo_ta: Guo Bao Rou is a classic Northeast Chinese dish originating from the Daotai Mansion in Harbin. It uses white vinegar to create a sharp, aromatic sourness, featuring a crispy exterior and tender meat slices. Pork provides high-quality protein, paired with ginger, onion, and vegetables to balance the richness. This dish requires mastering the starch coating, oil temperature, and double-frying technique. The difficulty is medium-high. Total time from marinating to serving is about 90 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Method two: potato starch 210g and all-purpose flour 70g
cac_buoc: **Process the pork**: Slice the pork loin into even 8mm thick slices, removing any white silver skin. Rinse the slices in water to remove blood. Optional: mix in 5g baking soda, let sit for 5 minutes, then rinse 1-2 times to remove excess soda.
**Marinate the meat**: Add 3g salt and 5ml cooking wine to the pork slices. Mix well and marinate for 15 minutes.

**Prepare the batter**: **Method one (recommended)**: Mix 170g potato starch with plenty of water. Let it sit for 60 minutes until the starch settles. Pour off all the top water, keeping the thick starch paste at the bottom. Add the pork slices, 5ml water, and 3ml oil. Mix well. **Method two**: Mix 210g potato starch and 70g all-purpose flour. Add water gradually until it reaches a yogurt-like consistency that ribbons when lifted. Add 10ml oil and 1g baking soda. Mix well. Coat each marinated pork slice thoroughly in the batter.

**Prepare the sweet and sour sauce**: Mix 65g sugar, 55g white vinegar, 4g light soy sauce, and 2g salt. Stir well and set aside. Optional: mix 4g water with 1.5g cornstarch to thicken the sauce later.
**Prepare aromatics**: Shred the green onion, ginger, and carrot. Cut cilantro into sections and slice the garlic.

**Fry the pork**: **First fry**: Heat oil to 170°C. Add pork slices one by one. Fry until the shape is set and the batter doesn't stick to chopsticks. The meat should float and be pale yellow (about 30 seconds). Remove and set aside. **Second fry**: Raise oil to 200°C. Fry all slices together until golden and crispy (about 30 seconds). Remove. **Third fry (optional)**: Raise oil to 220°C. Flash fry for 30 seconds until reddish-gold to maximize crispiness. Drain well.

**Stir-fry**: Keep 20ml of oil in the pan. Pour in the sauce and bring to a boil over high heat until thickened (30-60 seconds). Optional: set aside half the sauce for easier tossing. Add the fried pork, shredded onion, garlic, carrot, and cilantro. Drizzle the reserved sauce over and toss quickly 3 times to coat.
**Serve**: Transfer the Guo Bao Rou to a plate. Garnish with toasted sesame seeds (optional) and serve immediately.
**Notes**:
1. Meat slices must be 8mm thick; too thick or too thin will affect the texture.
2. Controlling oil temperature is crucial to prevent a dark or soggy crust.
3. Cook the sauce until syrupy but not clumped; avoid turning it into a hard candy.

mon_an.mo_ta: Steamed Pork Patty with Egg is a traditional home-style dish that is savory, fresh, and tender. The meat patty absorbs the juices, and the egg nestled inside is soft and silky—perfect with rice. It is rich in high-quality protein and amino acids. The method is extremely simple and very beginner-friendly, taking only about 20 minutes from prep to table.
cac_buoc: In a bowl, combine the ground pork, cooking wine, light soy sauce, white pepper powder, one egg, and sesame oil. Mix thoroughly.
Spread the seasoned ground pork evenly onto a plate. Use a spoon to make a small well in the center of the meat and crack the second egg into the hole.
Fill a steamer or pot with water to 1/4 height. Once the water boils, place the plate inside, cover, and steam for 15 minutes.
When removing the dish, be careful as the plate will be very hot.

mon_an.ten: Red Fermented Bean Curd Braised Pork (Phụ Nhũ Nhục)
mon_an.mo_ta: This is a classic Jiangnan home-style dish featuring pork belly braised with red fermented bean curd. The meat emerges with a glossy amber hue and a melt-in-the-mouth texture, releasing a harmonious blend of wine aroma and sweet-savory bean flavors. Rich in high-quality protein and B vitamins, the slow-simmering process makes it easy to digest. The recipe requires patience with heat control and sauce reduction, making it a slight challenge for beginners. Estimated cooking time is about 1 hour.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Before cooking, determine the number of servings. One serving is enough for about 2 people.
Red fermented bean curd 30 g (about 2 pieces)
cac_buoc: Cut the pork belly into small cubes, 2.5 cm wide and long.
Add cooking wine and ginger slices to cold water, add the pork belly, and bring to a boil; then remove the meat.
Mash the red fermented bean curd pieces with the brine into a smooth paste, then add rock sugar and dark soy sauce to make a sauce.
Heat the pan with oil and sauté the scallions and ginger until fragrant, then add the pork cubes and stir-fry until golden.
Pour in the bean curd sauce and stir-fry evenly, then add hot water to braise.
Simmer over low heat for 40 minutes.
Increase to high heat to reduce the sauce; when the sauce becomes thick with large bubbles, turn off the heat.
Single-crystal rock sugar is recommended.
Fermented bean curd is already salty and savory, so no extra salt is needed.
When reducing the sauce over high heat, constantly shake the pan to prevent sticking to the bottom.

mon_an.ten: Giant River Prawns with Mustard Sauce
mon_an.mo_ta: This dish is fragrant, fresh, and slightly spicy with a bold mustard aroma. The prawn meat is firm yet tender, making it a quick homemade seafood favorite. Prawns are rich in high-quality protein and calcium while being low in fat, and the mustard helps stimulate the appetite and cut through any richness. The difficulty is medium; by following the sauce preparation and heat control steps, even beginners can master it quickly. The entire process takes about 30 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Green mustard (wasabi) 20g, for the sauce bowl
Light soy sauce 30g, for the sauce bowl
Pepper powder 5g, for the sauce bowl
White sugar 3g, for the sauce bowl
Oyster sauce 15g, for the sauce bowl
cac_buoc: **Process the prawns**: Butterfly the prawns from the back, remove the vein and sand bag; you can also butterfly from the belly so they bloom beautifully when fried. Rinse with clean water and drain well; you may coat them in cornstarch or leave them plain.

**Prepare minced garlic and sauce bowl**: Mince 2 bulbs of garlic. Prepare the sauce bowl by mixing light soy sauce, oyster sauce, white sugar, pepper powder, and salt; squeeze in mustard to taste, add water to dilute, then stir in the cornstarch until dissolved.

**Stir-fry process**: Heat the pan and pour in cooking oil, enough to cover the bottom. Add the drained prawns and fry slowly. When the prawn oil is released (indicated by many bubbles in the pan), add the prepared minced garlic and bird's eye chili. Once the garlic is fragrant, add the butter. When the butter melts, stir well and pour in the prepared sauce bowl. Cover and simmer for 2 minutes; when the sauce thickens, remove from the pan and serve.
**Note**:
1. Do not fry for too long after adding the butter; once it melts and is stirred in, immediately add the sauce bowl.

mon_an.ten: Stir-fried Wild Rice Stems with Pork
mon_an.mo_ta: Stir-fried wild rice stems with pork is a quick home-style dish that is fresh, tender, and crunchy with a perfectly balanced savory flavor—a typical Jiangnan family taste. Wild rice stems are rich in fiber and vitamins, while lean pork provides high-quality protein for a nutritionally balanced meal. The difficulty is medium; beginners can master it with a little practice. Estimated cooking time is about 20 minutes.
cac_buoc: Preparation
Slice the wild rice stems into 0.5 cm thick pieces.
Cut the lean pork into strips 0.3-0.5 cm thick, then mix with cooking wine, starch, salt, and water.
Slice the ginger and mince the garlic. Cooking
Bring a pot of water to a boil, add the wild rice stems, cook for 60-90 seconds, then remove and drain.
Heat a pan with 15 ml of oil, add the lean pork, stir-fry continuously for 60 seconds, then remove.
Heat the pan again with 15 ml of oil, sauté the ginger and garlic for 30 seconds, then add the wild rice stems and stir-fry for another 30 seconds.
Add the pork back in and stir-fry for 60 seconds, add 20 ml of water, chicken bouillon powder, and salt, then stir-fry for 60 seconds before serving.
In the final step, you can consider using oyster sauce or light soy sauce instead of salt for better color.

mon_an.mo_ta: Lychee Pork is a traditional sweet and sour dish from Fuzhou (Fujian cuisine), featuring meat that is crispy on the outside and tender on the inside, coated in a glossy red sauce and paired with fruit for a refreshing aroma. Lean pork provides high-quality protein, while pineapple offers fiber and vitamins to help stimulate the appetite. The process involves specific cutting techniques, battering, and double-frying; it is a bit challenging but the steps are clear, making it suitable for food lovers with some cooking foundation. It takes about 45 minutes to bring to the table.
cac_buoc: Cut the lean pork into cubes (2-3 cm each), place in a large bowl, and add 1 egg, 50 g starch, 3 ml light soy sauce, and 2 g chicken bouillon powder.
Stir thoroughly until the starch coats the pork cubes (if too thin, add more starch; if too dry, add water), then add 5 ml oil, stir well, and set aside.
Prepare another bowl, mix ketchup, 3 g chicken bouillon powder, 2 ml light soy sauce, minced ginger, white sugar, 10 g starch, aromatic vinegar, and 200 ml cold water; stir well and set aside.
Cut a pineapple and prepare 6 pieces (1.5-2 cm each).
Heat 500 ml of oil in a pan until you hear a sizzling sound.
Add the pork pieces one by one into the pan (do not pour the whole bowl in), ensuring the pieces do not stick together.
After adding all the pork, use a spoon to flip the pieces every 30 seconds until the surface turns golden.
Remove the pork, wait one minute, then return it to the oil to fry again until the surface is golden-brown and crispy, then remove and set aside in a large bowl.
Heat the pan, pour in the sauce, and after 30 seconds, add the pork and pineapple pieces; stir-fry thoroughly and serve.
Garnish with sesame seeds.
Native Fuzhou people usually choose water chestnuts (to cut the richness) and potatoes (to absorb oil), but since they were unavailable during the pandemic, pineapple was chosen.
Fujian cuisine is primarily sweet; those not used to it can omit the white sugar.
You can tap the pork pieces with a spoon; the sound helps determine if the pork is fried through and crispy.

mon_an.ten: Stir-fried Snow Peas with Chinese Sausage
mon_an.mo_ta: Stir-fried snow peas with Chinese sausage is a refreshing and savory home-style dish where the fat from the sausage coats the bright green snow peas, making them crunchy and tender without being greasy. Snow peas are rich in high-quality protein and various vitamins, helping to boost the body's immunity. The method is simple, requiring almost no knife skills, so beginners can master it quickly. From preparation to serving, it takes only about 15 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: The following is a portion for one person.
cac_buoc: Trim the stems of the snow peas; if you have time, you can also trim the tails.
Before buying Chinese sausage, ask the seller if it is raw or cooked; if raw, it needs to be steamed first; if cooked, it can be used directly.
Wash the snow peas and blanch them for about 45 seconds until they change color, then remove and soak in cold water; set aside.
Heat the pan and add about 10 ml of cooking oil. Wait 10 seconds for the oil to heat up.
Add the Chinese sausage and stir-fry continuously until the edges *slightly curl*; be sure to **keep the heat very low** to prevent burning.
Add the snow peas, turn the heat to medium-high, stir-fry for 30 seconds, then add the light soy sauce and stir-fry for another 20-30 seconds.
Do not add salt during the process, as the sausage and light soy sauce are already salty.
Although Chinese sausage is delicious, it is a processed food; it is recommended to use it sparingly.

mon_an.mo_ta: This soup is clear and fresh without being greasy. The lamb is tender and flavorful, while the radish absorbs the sweet, mellow broth, becoming soft and succulent. It is a common warming family dish in Northern China during winter. Lamb is rich in high-quality protein and iron, while radish contains vitamins and fiber; together they nourish the spleen and stomach, dispel cold, and aid digestion. Although it requires blanching to remove gaminess and a two-stage stewing process, the steps are clear and easy to follow. The entire process takes about two hours, or can be shortened to one hour using a pressure cooker.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Water: enough to cover ingredients, about 1000ml
cac_buoc: Peel the radish and cut into large 3-5cm chunks; set aside.
When buying lamb ribs, ask the butcher to cut them for you as home knives are often not strong enough; set aside.
Place the lamb in a pot of cold water with half of the cooking wine and half of the ginger and leeks; boil for 10 minutes to remove the gamey smell, (optional) skim off any foam that rises.
In a separate pot of cold water, add the radish and half of the rock sugar; bring to a boil and cook for 5 minutes to remove the radish's bitterness.
Remove the blanched lamb ribs and place them in a pressure cooker; add enough water to cover the ingredients plus an extra 300ml.

Add the remaining leeks, ginger, cooking wine, Sichuan peppercorns, rock sugar, Angelica dahurica (optional), and salt; cover and bring to pressure, then simmer over medium heat for 15 minutes. If using a regular pot, simmer for 40 minutes to 1 hour.
Turn off the heat, wait for the pressure to release, open the lid, add the blanched radish, and adjust the seasoning with 3-10g of salt or water to taste.
Turn the heat back on to medium; once the pressure cooker reaches pressure, simmer for another 10 minutes (or 20 minutes for a regular pot).
Turn off the heat and serve.
During the process, monitor the water level; if it falls below 2/3 of the ingredients, add hot water to submerge them.

mon_an.mo_ta: Scallion braised chicken thighs is a savory, rice-pairing home dish that requires only two core ingredients: chicken thighs and large leeks. The chicken is crispy on the outside and tender on the inside with a deep scallion aroma. The method is simple, using only one pan, making it a guaranteed success for beginners. Rich in protein and perfect with rice, it is an ideal quick weekday dinner.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Before cooking, determine the number of servings. One serving is enough for 2 people.
Chicken thighs 2 pieces (about 350g of meat after deboning)
Dark soy sauce 5ml (for color; if unavailable, use more light soy sauce)
Oyster sauce 10ml (optional; if unavailable, add 5ml more light soy sauce)
cac_buoc: Debone the chicken thighs: use scissors to enter from the thick end of the thigh, cut the meat close to the bone, then make two cuts along the bone to separate the meat, and finally pull the bone out. This is safer than using a knife.
Cut the deboned chicken meat into 2-3cm cubes.
Slice the large leek into thick rounds (0.5cm thick) and cut the scallions into 1cm pieces.
Mix the chicken cubes with 10ml cooking wine, 5ml light soy sauce, 2g salt, and 1g white pepper; marinate for 10 minutes.
In a small bowl, mix the sauce: 10ml light soy sauce + 5ml dark soy sauce + 10ml oyster sauce + 5g sugar; set aside.
Heat the pan and add 15-20ml cooking oil.
Add ginger slices and Sichuan peppercorns; fry over low heat until the ginger is slightly browned and the peppercorns darken.
Use a slotted spoon to remove and discard the ginger and peppercorns, keeping the infused oil.
Over medium-high heat, spread the marinated chicken cubes in the pan; do not stir immediately.
Wait 2-3 minutes for the bottom of the chicken to develop a golden crust, then stir-fry until all sides change color and the chicken is fully cooked.
Add the sliced large leeks and stir-fry over medium-high heat for 1 minute to release the scallion aroma.
Pour in the prepared sauce, stir well, and cover with a lid.
Wait 2 minutes for the sauce and scallion aroma to fully infuse into the chicken.
Open the lid, add the scallion pieces and 2g of toasted white sesame seeds (optional), stir for 5-10 seconds, then turn off the heat and serve.
Tips for deboning chicken thighs (using scissors)
1. Wash the chicken thighs and pat the surface dry with paper towels.
2. Locate the bone end at the thicker part of the thigh.
3. Use the tip of the scissors to cut the skin and meat close to the bone, cutting all the way to the end along one side.
4. Flip the thigh and continue cutting along the other side of the bone.
5. Use your fingers to separate the meat from the bone joints.
6. Cut through the joints and pull the entire bone out.
This process requires no knife and is much safer than traditional methods; beginners can succeed on their first try.
Regarding "only scallions and chicken thighs"

The core of this dish is scallions and chicken, but using only those two lacks depth. The ginger, Sichuan peppercorns, oyster sauce, dark soy sauce, and sesame seeds used in the video are to make the flavors more multi-dimensional.
**Minimalist version**: scallions + chicken + salt + light soy sauce + sugar will work, but the flavor will be simple.
**Recommended version**: adding ginger, Sichuan peppercorns, and oyster sauce makes the flavor much richer.
**Perfect version**: adding dark soy sauce for color and toasted sesame seeds for garnish elevates both the appearance and taste.
Storage and Reheating
1. Refrigeration: seal in a container for up to 2 days.
2. Freezing: cool and portion before freezing; keeps for 1 month.
3. Reheating: microwave on medium for 2 minutes, or return to a pan with a little water and stir-fry.

mon_an.ten: Stir-fried Garlic Moss with Minced Pork
mon_an.mo_ta: Stir-fried garlic moss with minced pork is a Northern Chinese home-style dish that is savory, fresh, and crunchy with a bold garlic aroma. Garlic moss is rich in fiber and vitamins, while pork belly provides protein for a balanced meal. The method is simple and preparation is easy, making it very beginner-friendly. From cutting to serving, it takes only about 10 minutes.
cac_buoc: Cut the garlic moss into 5cm segments; set aside.
Cut the pork belly into 5mm * 5cm strips; set aside.
Crush and mince the garlic cloves; set aside.
Heat the pan and add 10ml of cooking oil. Wait 10 seconds for the oil to heat up.
Add the minced garlic and stir-fry over medium heat for **10 seconds** until fragrant.
Add the pork belly and 5ml of light soy sauce; stir-fry over medium heat for **30 seconds** until the meat is cooked and colored.
Add the garlic moss and 10ml of light soy sauce; stir-fry for **30 seconds**.
Add 20g of water to the pan and stir-fry over medium heat for **5 minutes** until the garlic moss softens slightly.
Finally, add 2g of salt and stir-fry over medium heat for **30 seconds**, then remove and serve on a plate.
Taste for seasoning before adding salt, and adjust the amount to your preference.
Thinly sliced pork belly is chosen because it is easy to cut and absorbs flavor well without marinating.

mon_an.ten: Tiger Skin Braised Pork Hock (Hổ Bì Chửu Tử)
mon_an.mo_ta: The finished dish features a glossy red color and an attractive 'tiger skin' texture on the rind. It is tender, flavorful, and rich without being greasy, with meat that pulls apart easily—a traditional Chinese banquet centerpiece. Pork hock is rich in collagen and high-quality protein, which becomes easily absorbable after long stewing, providing benefits for skin and joints. The process involves multiple steps including skin-scorching, frying, caramelizing sugar, and pressure cooking. It is quite challenging for beginners; it is recommended for those with a cooking foundation. Total time from prep to table is approximately 2.5 hours.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Vegetable oil: enough to submerge 3/5 of the hock (by height)
cac_buoc: Pre-processing
After thawing the pork hock, soak it in water for 1 hour to remove blood.

If you have a kitchen torch, burn the surface of the **pork skin** until it is **dark brown** to remove hair and break down the pores. Do not roast one spot for too long to avoid charring; stop when the skin is almost entirely dark brown.

If no torch is available, heat a cast-iron pan to over 200°C, place the hock directly in the pan, and use a spatula or chopsticks to ensure the skin makes full contact with the surface. When the skin turns brown, rotate to another spot until the entire hock is seared. Monitor the pan temperature so it doesn't turn glowing red.
Use a scouring pad to scrub the hock in water, removing the charred surface. After scrubbing, the hock should return to its original color.
Place the hock in a cast-iron pan and add as much cold water as possible, ensuring it covers at least 3/4 of the hock. Blanching
Take the white part of 1 scallion, cut into 3 segments, and add to the pan.
Take 3 cloves of garlic, crush them with the side of a knife, and add to the pan.
Add 3 grams of ginger to the pan.
Add 2 tbsp of cooking wine to the pan.
Once the water boils, wait five minutes, then remove the hock. Discard the aromatics but set aside the meat broth for later use. Frying
Add oil to the pan. Use enough to submerge 3/5 of the hock. Heat over medium heat.
When the oil is moderately hot, turn to low heat and add the hock to fry.
Exercise caution for personal safety during frying.
During frying, use a spatula or heat-resistant tool to continuously ladle hot oil over the exposed parts of the hock. If possible, flip the hock every 3 minutes for even frying.
Fry for about 20 minutes until the skin is light brown and the meat is slightly seared, then remove and set aside.
The oil can be reused for other frying, but do not reuse it too many times. Caramelizing
Use the 200 ml of rock sugar to make a caramel sauce; set aside. Stewing

Place the hock in a pressure cooker. Add the meat broth, caramel sauce, bay leaves, cinnamon, cardamom, Sichuan peppercorns, star anise, dark soy sauce, light soy sauce, and white vinegar. If you prefer it sweeter, add 2-3 grams of rock sugar.
Add 3 segments of scallion white to the pot.
Add 3 crushed garlic cloves to the pot.
Add 3 grams of ginger to the pot.
Cover and pressure cook for 40 minutes. Reducing the Sauce
While stewing, prepare a starch slurry. Mix 1 tbsp starch with 100ml water into a cloudy white liquid.
When the time is up, open the pressure cooker and remove all aromatics, leaving only the hock.
Transfer the remaining broth to a cast-iron pan and move the hock to a serving plate.
Place the pan on the stove over high heat. During reduction, taste the sauce and add salt as needed. Note that the flavor will intensify as the sauce reduces.
Monitor the liquid level as it boils.
When the liquid has reduced to less than half its original volume, restir the starch slurry and pour in half.
Wait for it to boil, then add the remaining half.
Let it boil for 1-2 minutes until it becomes a thick, reddish-brown glaze, then turn off the heat.
Use a spoon to ladle the sauce evenly over the hock, ensuring every part is coated. Serve immediately.

mon_an.ten: Ants Climbing a Tree (Mã Nghị Thượng Thụ)
mon_an.mo_ta: 'Ants Climbing a Tree' is a classic Sichuan home-style dish that is savory, fragrant, and slightly spicy. The vermicelli is soft and slippery, having absorbed the sauce, while the finely minced pork provides fresh, savory bits. The main ingredients are sweet potato vermicelli and minced pork, providing quick energy through starch and protein. The difficulty is medium with clear steps, making it friendly for beginners. The entire process takes about 20 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Before cooking, determine the number of servings. One serving is enough for 2 people.
cac_buoc: Soak the sweet potato vermicelli in water for 20 minutes until soft, then set aside.
Mince the garlic and ginger separately; set aside.
Heat the pan, add 10ml oil, and sauté the minced garlic and ginger until fragrant.
Add the minced pork and stir-fry until the **meat turns white and starts to release fat**.
Add the Pixian doubanjiang and stir-fry until the **red oil is released**.
Add the light and dark soy sauces, and stir well.
Pour in 300ml of water and bring to a boil.
Add the soaked and drained vermicelli, using chopsticks to gently separate the strands to prevent sticking.
Cook over medium-low heat for about 5 minutes until the vermicelli **completely absorbs the sauce** and the pan is nearly dry.
Optionally garnish with chopped scallions, turn off the heat, and serve.
Do not overcook the vermicelli as it will break easily and lose its texture; if cooking longer, reduce the amount of sauce accordingly.
Pixian doubanjiang is very salty, so you may reduce the light soy sauce to taste.
You can add 0.5g of white pepper powder for extra flavor.

mon_an.mo_ta: Blood Duck is a famous traditional dish from Wugang, Hunan: the duck meat is fragrant, crispy, and tender. After absorbing the blood vinegar, even the ginger and chilies become sweet and mild. Duck meat and duck blood provide high-quality protein and iron, making it excellent for nourishing the blood. Although there are many steps and it requires careful heat control and constant stirring, beginners can complete it in about 2 hours by following the instructions.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Ginger 6 slices (add 1-3 more slices depending on spice preference)
Green onions 2 stalks, chopped and set aside
Chilies 1000g (choose green chilies, shredded chilies, or beauty chilies; for more heat, add 5-8 bird's eye chilies, chopped and set aside)
cac_buoc: Cut the fresh young duck into small pieces of about 3cm. Add cooking wine and ginger slices to remove any blood residue.
Heat a wok, add about 100ml of cooking oil, wait for the oil to boil over high heat, then add the marinated duck and stir-fry continuously.

When the duck meat completely changes color (turning white to the eye), pour in the alcohol, then add 200ml of boiling water (just enough to cover the duck). Cover and cook over medium heat for 15 minutes.
Once boiling, open the lid, add the ginger and garlic, stir once, then cover and continue to cook for 10 minutes.

Open the lid and add the chilies. Stir-fry continuously until the chilies soften, then pour in the fresh duck blood. At this point, you must stir constantly to ensure every piece of duck and chili is thoroughly coated in blood (this is the essence of Blood Duck).
Stir-fry until the duck blood turns black. Add salt, chicken bouillon, and green onions (if you like litsea oil, you can add 3-6 drops now). Stir once or twice more.
Remove from the pot and serve on a plate to enjoy.
While cooking, monitor the water level and adjust the heat to prevent the sauce from drying out and sticking to the pan.
When adding the fresh duck blood, stir continuously to prevent it from clumping or curdling into blocks.

mon_an.mo_ta: A sweet and sour home-style stew with a rich sauce, tender beef, and fluffy potatoes. Beef provides high-quality protein, tomatoes are rich in lycopene, and combined with potatoes and onions, it offers balanced nutrition. The process is simple with no complex techniques required, making it easy for beginners. It takes about 1 to 1.5 hours from preparation to serving.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Green onion 1 stalk, ginger 4 slices, cooking wine
Oil 15ml (reduce to 10ml if using beef brisket, depending on preference)
Soy sauce (additive-free light soy sauce), dark soy sauce
Black pepper powder (white pepper is also fine) 2g
Potatoes 2-3 (depending on preference, enough to fit the pot)
cac_buoc: Preparation: Peel the potatoes and cut into large 5cm chunks; set aside. Score a cross on the tomatoes, blanch in boiling water, peel, remove the core, and cut into 3cm pieces; set aside. Finely chop 4g of green onion; cut the rest into 5-8cm lengths. Soak the beef in cold water for 30 minutes to remove blood, or place in a pot of cold water and cook until the surface turns white, then remove and skim off the foam. Finely dice the onion into 0.5-1cm pieces.

Cooking: Maintain medium heat throughout. Cover the beef with cold water in a pressure cooker, add the green onion sections, ginger slices, and 20g of cooking wine. Once pressurized, cook for 20 minutes. Remove the beef and cut into large 5cm chunks; discard the ginger. Pour the broth into a large bowl to use for stewing later. Heat oil; when it reaches 40-50% heat, add Sichuan peppercorns, star anise, and bay leaves. Once fragrant and before they burn, remove and discard them. Add the beef, onion, and ginger and sauté until fragrant. If it starts to scorch, add 10ml of broth; repeat as needed. Once fragrant, add 15ml light soy sauce, 15ml cooking wine, pepper powder, 5-10g tomato paste (or tomato sauce/canned tomatoes). Add the diced onion and sauté until translucent (optional: add a pinch of salt to help the onion release moisture and prevent burning). Add the tomatoes and sauté until they break down, then pour in the remaining broth.

Stewing: Bring to a boil over medium heat, then simmer on low heat. 30-40 minutes before finishing, add the potatoes and season. Adjust with sugar and salt to taste. When the beef is tender enough to be pierced easily with a chopstick, it is ready!
Ensure the broth is warm when adding it back for stewing.
Do not cover the lid tightly while stewing, or the potatoes will turn to mush.
Stir occasionally while stewing to prevent burning the bottom.
Stewing in a clay pot tastes better; you can sauté in a pan then transfer to a clay pot. If using a clay pot, do not use high heat before it boils to avoid cracking.
Do not use too much soy sauce; the sauce will become saltier as it reduces. It is fine if it tastes a bit light when thin. You can add more soy sauce later if needed.
Do not use chicken bouillon or MSG, as they will overpower the natural freshness of the beef.

mon_an.mo_ta: Tomato beef brisket features a thick, sweet, and sour sauce with tender, fragrant beef. It is an appetizing home-style dish that pairs perfectly with rice. Rich in protein, vitamins, and lycopene, it offers balanced nutrition. It is slightly challenging for beginners, requiring mastery of meat stewing heat and sautéing tomato sauce. Beginners usually need about 90 minutes to complete it.
cac_buoc: Cut the beef brisket into 2cm cubes. Place in a pot of cold water, bring to a boil, and cook for 2 minutes to remove blood. Remove and rinse clean.

In another pot, bring 2L of water to a boil. Add two 2cm sections of green onion, two ginger slices, star anise, and 5-10ml of cooking wine/yellow wine. Add the blanched beef, cover, and simmer (1 hour for a clay pot, 45 minutes for a pressure cooker on meat mode) until a chopstick can easily pierce the meat.

Peel the tomatoes: Score a cross on the top. Insert a fork or chopstick into the stem end and rotate over a low gas flame. Remove as soon as the skin starts to peel, then strip off the skin and cut into very small pieces. Be careful of the heat and the slippery texture after peeling; cut slowly for safety.

Heat oil in a pan until 70% hot. Add 10g each of green onion and ginger, then add the tomatoes. Sauté until the oil turns red, then add the cooked brisket and enough of the original beef broth to just cover the meat.
Season with salt, sugar, and light soy sauce to taste, then cover.
Once boiling, continue to cook over high heat for 3-5 minutes.
When the tomato sauce has reached a medium thickness, turn off the heat, sprinkle with chopped green onions, and serve.
Pay close attention to fire safety throughout the process.
When stewing meat in a clay or aluminum pot, turn the heat to medium-low/low after boiling. If using a pressure cooker, follow the manual's instructions.
The roasting method for peeling tomatoes described here is the fastest practical method.
Avoid using ketchup and use minimal spices to preserve the original flavor of the ingredients.

mon_an.ten: Stir-fried Lettuce with Canned Dace and Black Beans
mon_an.mo_ta: This is a quick, savory, and fragrant home-style stir-fry inspired by Cantonese canned food. The long-leaf lettuce is crisp and refreshing, while the dace is fragrant and crunchy. This meat-and-vegetable combination is rich in protein and fiber. The method is simple and very beginner-friendly, usually taking only fifteen minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Canned dace with salted black beans 1 can (approx. 250g)
cac_buoc: **Ingredient Preparation**: Wash the lettuce and cut into sections. Open the can of dace, remove the main spine of the fish, and cut into small pieces; set aside. Mince the garlic.

**Stir-frying Process**: Heat a wok and add cooking oil. When the oil is hot, add the lettuce. Stir-fry until wilted and it releases some water, then remove the lettuce and set aside, discarding the excess liquid. Reheat the wok, add the oil from the dace can, and sauté the minced garlic until fragrant. Add the black beans from the can, stir, then add the chopped dace and stir again. Once well mixed, return the lettuce to the wok and season with light soy sauce and sugar. Toss briefly to combine, then remove from the pot and serve.
**Note**:
1. Canned dace is already seasoned; the light soy sauce should provide enough flavor, so no extra salt is needed.

mon_an.ten: Steamed Spare Ribs with Black Beans
mon_an.mo_ta: This is a popular dish in Cantonese teahouses, featuring a rich black bean aroma and ribs so tender they fall off the bone. Spare ribs provide high-quality protein and calcium, while fermented black beans add flavor and are easier to digest. The method involves soaking, marinating, and controlled steaming. It is slightly challenging for beginners, but the steps are clear. It takes about 1 hour from prep to serving. The leftover sauce is delicious mixed with rice or noodles.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine the number of servings before starting. One serving is enough for 2-4 people.
Cooking oil 20 ml (use 10 ml if not drizzling hot oil at the end)
cac_buoc: Soak the ribs in cold water for 10 minutes to remove blood. Change the water and repeat twice, then pat dry with paper towels.
Soak the black beans in water for 5 minutes.
Mix all ingredients together (using only 10 ml of the oil) and marinate for 8-30 minutes.
Once the water is boiling, steam for 18 minutes.
Let it rest for 2 minutes.
Heat 10 ml of oil in a pan to 180-200 ℃.
Sprinkle chopped green onions and white sesame seeds over the ribs, then drizzle the hot oil over them.
Lightly mashing the black beans after soaking will release more flavor.
Adjust steaming time based on the size of the ribs; they are done when a chopstick can easily pierce the cartilage.
Traditional Cantonese steamed ribs do not usually include the garnish and hot oil drizzle.
The leftover sauce is excellent for mixing with rice or noodles.

mon_an.ten: Steamed White Eel with Black Beans
mon_an.mo_ta: A classic Cantonese steamed dish where the savory black bean and garlic sauce infuses the fish, resulting in a tender and fresh texture. White eel is rich in high-quality protein and unsaturated fatty acids, making it very nourishing. The steps are clear, but handling live fish and mastering the heat can be challenging, making it suitable for those with some cooking experience. Takes about 30 minutes from prep to table.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: White eel 250g (approx. one small eel, gutted and sliced)
Green onion 1 stalk (cut into sections or shreds)
cac_buoc: **Check and wash the eel**: Ensure the fishmonger has gutted, deslimed, and cut the eel into 5cm sections. At home, check the eel and rinse thoroughly to ensure no slime or impurities remain. Optional: Rub the eel sections with 3g salt and 1 tsp cornstarch, let sit for 5 minutes, then rinse to remove fishiness and increase tenderness.

**Prepare the sauce**: In a small bowl, mix 1 tbsp black beans, 2 minced garlic cloves, 1.5 tbsp light soy sauce, 0.5 tsp dark soy sauce, 0.5 tsp sugar, 0.5 tsp sesame oil, and 1 tbsp water. Stir well. For a stronger flavor, add an extra 0.5 tbsp of black beans.
**Plating**: Arrange the eel sections flat on a heatproof plate, trying not to overlap them. Sprinkle the shredded ginger evenly over the eel. Drizzle the prepared black bean sauce over the top.

**Steaming**: Add water (500ml) to a steamer or electric food steamer and bring to a boil. Place the plate of eel inside and cover. Steam over medium-high heat for 8-10 minutes (adjust based on the thickness of the eel) until the meat turns white and no blood remains.

**Garnish and Finish**: Once steamed, remove from the heat. Garnish with shredded green onions and red chili (optional). You can drizzle with a little hot sesame oil to enhance the aroma. Serve hot with white rice.
**Notes**:
Ensure the eel is fresh; live fish provides much more tender meat.
You can ask the fishmonger to cut the sections to about 5cm for easier steaming and eating.
Do not over-steam, or the eel meat will become tough.
**Variations**:
Add fresh chilies or XO sauce for extra spice and depth of flavor.
For a silkier texture, add a little rice wine during marination.

mon_an.mo_ta: A classic home-style dish from Guizhou made with 'Ciba' pounded chilies and various aromatics. The chicken is fragrant and tender, while the potatoes are fluffy and flavorful. The overall taste is intensely spicy and savory. Chicken provides high-quality protein, and with potatoes, it is a balanced meal. This dish has many steps and is a bit challenging for beginners, but following the sequence will lead to success. Expect about 1.5 hours from prep to serving.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Chicken: 2kg for 3-4 people (scale up for more people)
Ciba chili (pounded chili) 500g (about two fist-sized lumps)
Rapeseed oil 1kg (a large amount is needed for frying)
cac_buoc: Fill a wok halfway with oil. First, fry the potato wedges until the surface is golden, then remove and set aside. Wait for the oil to reach a high heat, then add the chopped chicken, ginger slices, and Sichuan peppercorns to fry.
Initially, the oil will be cloudy due to the moisture in the chicken. Fry until the oil becomes clear again, indicating the chicken is done, then remove and set aside.
Remove about one-third of the oil from the wok; you don't need that much for the next steps.
Heat the remaining oil, add the Ciba chili, bean paste, and ginger slices. Sauté until the oil turns red, then add the fried chicken and toss to coat.
Once the chicken is well-colored, add dark soy sauce and pour in the beer (the beer must cover the chicken). Add bay leaves, cover, and simmer for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the potato wedges and whole garlic cloves (best kept whole), then simmer for another 20 minutes.
Finally, add fermented glutinous rice (jiuniang), stir well, then add the chopped leeks and serve.
Stir frequently during the process as the pounded chilies burn easily.

mon_an.mo_ta: A flavorful Hunan home-style dish featuring charred chilies and tender, savory pork slices. It is salty, fresh, and spicy—a perfect 'rice killer.' Pork provides high-quality protein and B vitamins, while green chilies offer plenty of Vitamin C. This dish requires mastery of dry-frying and quick stir-frying, suitable for those with some cooking experience. Takes about 30 minutes from prep to serving.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Determine the number of servings before starting. One serving is enough for 1 person.
Calculate the ingredient ratios based on these conditions.
cac_buoc: Wash the `green chilies`, remove the `stems` and `seeds`, then `roll-cut` them and set aside.
Smash the `garlic` with a knife and chop into `cloves`; finely mince the `fresh ginger`.
Slice the `lean pork` into `slices` (cut parallel to the grain so the slices show a visual pattern of three vertical lines).
Rinse the sliced `pork`, place in a bowl, and mix with the calculated `light soy sauce`, `oyster sauce`, and `salt`. Marinate for 10 minutes.
Heat a wok without oil. Add the `cut green chilies` and stir-fry over high heat until they develop 'tiger skin' char marks. Add 2g of `salt`, continue stir-frying for 1 minute, then remove.
Without washing the wok, heat it over high heat. Add servings * 8ml of `oil`, wait 30 seconds, then add the `garlic` and `minced ginger` and sauté for 15 seconds.
Add the marinated `pork` to the wok and stir-fry for 2 minutes, then add the dry-fried `green chilies` and stir-fry for 1 minute.
Add `black beans` to taste, and finally add the `dark soy sauce`. Stir-fry for another 30 seconds.
Remove from the pot and serve on a plate.
**Only use green chilies; spiral chilies are the best choice. Do not use other types of chilies!**!

mon_an.ten: Braised Spare Ribs in Bean Sauce
mon_an.mo_ta: These ribs have a deep reddish-brown color, tender meat, and a rich, savory-sweet sauce. It is a classic home-style dish. Spare ribs are rich in protein and calcium. This dish involves caramelizing sugar and a long braising time, which can be challenging for beginners, but following the steps will ensure success. Expect about 1 hour from prep to serving.
cac_buoc: Bring a pot of water to a boil. Add the ribs, ginger slices, and cooking wine. Once boiling, skim off the white foam. After 2-3 minutes, remove the ribs.
Rinse the ribs with cold water 2-3 times.
Heat a pan over low heat, add oil and white sugar. Stir gently until the sugar turns golden brown.
Add the ribs and stir-fry for 30 seconds. Add light soy sauce, oyster sauce, five-spice powder, garlic, and bird's eye chili. Stir-fry for 30 seconds, then add enough water to cover the ribs.
Cook over high heat for 30 minutes. Add dark soy sauce for color, then cook for another 10 minutes.
Remove from the pan and plate.
To enhance the flavor, consider adding bean paste or tomato sauce.
The high-heat cooking time can be adjusted based on your preference.
While the ribs are cooking, you can add 2-3 eggs to the pot to make simple braised eggs.

mon_an.ten: Braised Beef Shank in Bean Sauce
mon_an.mo_ta: A savory Northern-style cold dish with a rich bean aroma and a firm, chewy texture. Beef shank is rich in protein and amino acids, and slow-braising makes it easier to digest. The process is not overly complex but involves marinating, slow-braising, and long refrigeration. Beginners will need patience; the total time is about 10 hours.
cac_buoc: Wash the beef shank and soak in clean water for 1 hour to remove blood.
Use a toothpick or fork to poke holes in the surface of the beef. Add cooking wine, Sichuan peppercorns, and ginger slices. Cover with plastic wrap and marinate for 4-6 hours.
Cut the beef shank into 8cm blocks (no larger than 10cm).
Place the beef in a pot and add cold water until covered. Start timing once the water boils, and skim off the foam. After 3 minutes, turn off the heat, remove the beef, and rinse with warm water.
Place the rinsed beef in a clay pot or stew pot. Add water to cover the beef, turn to high heat, and add all remaining ingredients except the salt.
Once boiling, turn the heat to low and simmer for 90 minutes, then add the salt.
After adding salt, continue to simmer on low for another 90 minutes (Note: check the water level every 30 minutes; it should cover at least 80% of the beef).
After 180 minutes of total cooking, remove the beef, wrap it tightly in plastic wrap, and refrigerate for several hours.
Once chilled, slice against the grain and serve. It is recommended to keep the remaining beef refrigerated until ready to slice.
Monitor the water level while boiling; if it falls below 2/3 of the ingredients, add hot water to submerge them (check roughly every 30 minutes).
Wrapping the beef tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerating it for several hours ensures the meat is firm and does not fall apart when sliced.
Poking holes in the surface of the beef helps break down the connective tissue and allows the flavors to penetrate better.

mon_an.mo_ta: Drunken Pork Ribs is a famous traditional dish from Fuzhou, crispy on the outside and tender on the inside with a sweet and sour appetizer profile and the unique savory taste of fish sauce. Ribs are rich in protein and calcium, making them both nutritious and satisfying. This dish requires mastering coating and double-frying techniques, making it suitable for those with some cooking experience. The entire process takes about 40 minutes.
cac_buoc: Mix 5 g of sweet potato starch and water with the ribs, wash 2-3 times, then place in a large bowl and set aside.
Add the fish sauce, sweet potato starch, and egg yolk to the ribs and mix thoroughly.
Place each rib piece individually into the pan (do not pour the whole bowl in) to ensure the pieces do not stick together.
After adding all the ribs, use a spoon to flip them every 30 seconds until the surface turns golden.
Remove the ribs, wait one minute, then return them to the oil to fry again until the surface becomes a charred golden brown, then remove and set aside in a large bowl.
Prepare a small bowl, mix the minced garlic, aromatic vinegar, white sugar, fish sauce, ketchup, chopped green onions, and sesame seeds together, then pour in 5 ml of hot oil.
Drizzle the sauce over the ribs, toss thoroughly, and serve on a plate.
Fish sauce (yu lu), also known as fish soy sauce, is a common seasoning in Guangdong and Fujian... Its effect is similar to light soy sauce.
In this preparation, due to the pandemic, fish sauce was unavailable so dark soy sauce was used as a substitute, resulting in a darker color; normally it should be golden yellow.

mon_an.ten: Stir-fried Pork with Green Peppers and Potatoes
mon_an.mo_ta: Stir-fried Pork with Green Peppers and Potatoes is a classic family-style stir-fry combining meat and vegetables. It is fresh, crispy, and tender with a rich savory aroma, making it a perfect companion for rice. Potatoes are rich in starch and vitamin C, green peppers provide plenty of vitamin C and fiber, and combined with high-quality pork protein, it offers balanced nutrition. The method is not complicated and is beginner-friendly, taking about 1 hour from preparation to serving.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Before each preparation, determine how many servings you intend to make. One serving is enough for 2 people.
cac_buoc: Remove the stems from the green peppers and cut into small pieces; peel the potatoes and slice thinly into 2mm pieces; slice the pork into 4mm thin pieces; cut the green onion into 3mm segments; peel and mince the ginger and garlic; mix the potato starch with 15g of water to make a slurry.
Heat oil in a wok until it reaches 70% heat, then add the pork slices. Stir-fry slowly until the meat is no longer red, add about 3ml of soy sauce to color the meat evenly, and add about 2g of salt.

Lower the oil temperature to 50% heat, add the onion, ginger, and garlic and sauté for 5 seconds. Then add the potato slices, raise the heat back to 70%, and stir-fry evenly. Add about 5ml of soy sauce and 2g of salt, stir-frying until the potatoes are just cooked and the surface is slightly charred.

Raise the heat to 80% and add the green peppers. Stir-fry on high heat to achieve "wok hei" (until white smoke appears), stirring continuously for 1 minute to develop color. Finally, pour the starch slurry around the edge of the pan and lower to 40% heat to thicken.
Once the exterior reaches a *thickened state*, turn off the heat and serve on a plate.

mon_an.mo_ta: This classic Guangxi family dish uses green peppers stuffed with seasoned minced meat or shrimp paste, pan-fried until the skin is blistered into a "tiger skin" pattern, then braised to absorb the flavors. The fresh aroma of the peppers blends with the savory filling for a salty, fragrant, and slightly spicy dish that goes great with rice. Pork and shrimp provide quality protein, while green peppers are rich in vitamin C. Stuffing requires some patience, but the process is clear and usually takes 30 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Green peppers 8 (about 400g, choose straight, thick-fleshed peppers)
Light soy sauce 30ml (15ml for the filling, 15ml for the sauce)
Starch 10g (optional: 5g to coat the inside of peppers, 5g for the slurry)
cac_buoc: Prepare the filling.
Wash and finely mince the pork (or use a meat grinder), mince the ginger, and finely chop the green onions.
Add the minced ginger, green onions, 15ml light soy sauce, 5ml dark soy sauce, and 3g salt to the minced meat; mix well.
Optional additions: 10ml cooking wine, 10ml oyster sauce, 1 egg, 5g starch, 2g white pepper powder, 5g white sugar.
Stir the meat filling in one direction until it becomes thick and sticky, then marinate for 10 minutes. Process the green peppers.
Wash the green peppers, remove the stems, and carefully use a chopstick to remove the seeds and white ribs inside, keeping the pepper intact.
Optional: Sprinkle about 5g of dry starch inside the peppers and shake well to help the meat filling stick. Stuff the filling.
Use chopsticks or a piping bag to stuff the marinated meat into the green peppers; try to fill them completely but not too tightly to avoid bursting.
Once stuffed, set aside. Prepare the sauce.
In a bowl, mix 15ml light soy sauce, 5ml dark soy sauce, and 100ml water.
Optional: Add 5g of starch to make the sauce thicker. Pan-fry and braise.
Heat the pan, pour in 30ml oil, and when the oil is 50-60% hot, add the stuffed peppers (meat side down first).
Fry slowly over medium-low heat, flipping them so all sides are fried until the skin is blistered and "tiger-skinned," then remove and set aside.
Keep the remaining oil in the pan; optionally add minced garlic and sauté until fragrant.
Pour in the prepared sauce and bring to a boil, then add the fried peppers.
Lower the heat to medium-low, cover, and braise for 5-8 minutes until the sauce thickens and the peppers are soft.
Open the lid and turn to high heat to reduce the sauce until it is glossy and coats the peppers, then remove and serve. Shrimp paste version.
Peel 250g of shrimp and remove the veins, use the back of a knife to smash into a paste (keep some texture for better mouthfeel; or buy pre-made shrimp paste).
Season the shrimp: 5g minced ginger, 2g salt, 5g starch, 10ml light soy sauce.
Optional: 5ml cooking wine, 1g white pepper, half an egg white.
Stir in one direction until sticky, marinate for 10 minutes.
Follow the same stuffing, frying, and braising steps as the pork version.
Shrimp cooks quickly, so braising time can be shortened to 4-5 minutes.
Choosing straight peppers makes stuffing easier than curved ones; thick-fleshed peppers taste better than thin-skinned ones.
Stir the filling in one direction to ensure it is springy and firm.
Dusting the inside with dry starch is key to preventing the filling from falling out during frying.
Frying until the skin is blistered is the source of the flavor; do not skip this step.
Adjust the sauce to taste; if you like it spicier, add Guilin chili sauce.
Shrimp and pork fillings can be mixed in any ratio; shrimp adds sweetness while pork adds richness.
The sauce is excellent with rice; do not reduce it until completely dry.

mon_an.ten: Stir-fried Shredded Pork with Smoked Tofu (Xiang Gan Rou Si)
mon_an.mo_ta: Xiang Gan Rou Si is a savory family-style stir-fry that goes perfectly with rice. It features tender shredded pork, chewy smoked tofu, and crispy green peppers. It is rich in both animal and plant proteins, with green peppers providing vitamins. The difficulty is moderate; beginners can master it with a little practice. Estimated cooking time is about 30 minutes.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Before each preparation, determine how many servings you intend to make. One serving is enough for 1 person.
Calculate the ingredient ratios based on the above conditions.
cac_buoc: Preparation.
Mix the `shredded pork` (cut it yourself if not pre-shredded) with light soy sauce (3ml) and starch; set aside.
Wash the `green peppers`, then use the `roll-cutting technique` to prepare them; set aside.
Slice the `garlic` crosswise and cut the `smoked tofu` into strips.
Mix the `starch` with water (10ml) and stir well. Stir-fry.
Add 15ml oil to a clean pan; without waiting for the oil to get hot, add the shredded pork and gently separate the strands. Once the pork is cooked, remove immediately, keeping the oil in the pan.
Add the garlic slices and smoked tofu to the pan, add 2ml light soy sauce, and stir-fry evenly.
After 2-3 minutes, depending on the heat, add the green pepper strips to the pan and stir-fry.
After 1 minute, add the pork back in and toss together.
Pour in the starch slurry to thicken, add 3g salt and 2g chicken powder, stir-fry for 2-3 minutes, then serve.
Finished. Note: different pans or stoves will affect cooking time; if unsure if it is cooked, you can perform a taste test.
**For the peppers, choose green peppers or twist peppers; if you like it spicy, add chopped bird's eye chilies at the same time as the green peppers!**

mon_an.ten: Stir-fried Pork with Smoked Tofu and Celery
mon_an.mo_ta: Stir-fried Pork with Smoked Tofu and Celery is a family-style stir-fry: chewy tofu, crunchy celery, and tender pork with a savory and slightly spicy flavor. Celery is rich in fiber, while smoked tofu and pork provide quality plant and animal proteins. The method is simple and beginner-friendly, taking about 30 minutes from preparation to serving.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Note: this amount serves about 2 people.
Sichuan peppercorns: 6 (optional, or use Sichuan pepper water)
cac_buoc: Remove leaves from the celery and cut into segments no longer than 4cm; set aside.
Cut the smoked tofu into strips about the width of a pinky finger; set aside.
Slice or mince the garlic; set aside.
Cut the chilies into rings or diagonal strips; set aside.
Heat the pan and add 10ml - 15ml of cooking oil. Wait 10 seconds for the oil to heat up.
Add the Sichuan peppercorns and garlic and sauté until fragrant (if you like ginger, you can also add some sliced or shredded ginger).
Add the pork and stir-fry until it changes color, then add 8ml dark soy sauce for color and toss evenly (if you have doubanjiang, you can add 3ml and stir-fry together).
Add the smoked tofu and stir-fry evenly (about 2 minutes).
Add the chilies and stir-fry evenly (about 1-2 minutes).
Add the celery and 5g salt, then stir-fry for 1 minute.
Add 3g chicken powder and 5ml oyster sauce, toss well, and serve.
If you cannot find Chinese celery or if the celery is quite thick, consider blanching it in boiling water for 1 minute, then rinsing with cold water to maintain crunchiness.
If the smoked tofu you bought is quite hard or firm, you can also cut it into strips and blanch it briefly.

mon_an.ten: Pan-Seared Pork Belly (Xiang Xian Wu Hua Rou)
mon_an.mo_ta: Pan-seared pork belly is a quick and savory home-style dish. The slices are seared until fragrant and slightly crispy, offering a rich but non-greasy taste. Combined with cool, crisp lettuce and fresh soybean paste, the bold flavors perfectly balance the richness of the meat. Pork is high in quality protein and fat for a quick energy boost, while lettuce provides fiber and vitamins for balanced nutrition. This dish is suitable for those with basic cooking skills; beginners just need to manage the heat and watch out for oil splashes. It takes about 30 minutes from preparation to serving.
nguyen_lieu_dung_cu: Before each preparation, determine how many servings to make. One serving is enough for 1 person.
cac_buoc: Slice the pork belly block lengthwise into slices 1mm-1.5mm thick, then set aside
Place the sliced pork belly in a bowl and marinate for 10 minutes with 8g soy sauce, 1g salt, 1g MSG, 10g cooking wine, two slices of ginger, and two smashed garlic cloves
Tear the lettuce leaves by hand, wash thoroughly, and set aside
Heat the pan and add 5ml cooking oil. When the oil starts to smoke slightly, add the pork belly. Sear one side until golden brown, then flip and do the same for the other side.
Once the pork belly is done, remove from the pan and arrange on a plate.
Spread soybean paste on a lettuce leaf, wrap a slice of pork belly inside, and enjoy
Be careful during cooking to avoid burns from oil splashes

mon_an.ten: Tender Chicken with Shiitake Mushrooms (Xiang Gu Huo Ji)
